title: AI-ConneX Master Architecture Specification
summary: Master system specification governing global architecture, infrastructure topology, security boundaries, and high-availability SLAs.

sections.content:
AI-ConneX Platform

Master Architecture Specification & Technical Blueprint

Total Automation Solutions (TAS) | Industrial AI Platform EngineeringData Studio • ML Studio • Agentic StudioVersion 1.0 — Master Specification | August 2026

The AI-ConneX Master Architecture Specification represents a unified technical blueprint for enterprise industrial AI deployment. Designed to bridge the gap between raw plant telemetry and intelligent automated reasoning, AI-ConneX establishes three bounded, microservice-ready execution studios: Data Studio (deterministic data integration, profiling, and recipe compilation), ML Studio (the S.T.E.M. training and evaluation spine), and Agentic Studio (human-grounded visual intelligence, blueprint specification, and tool execution). This master specification compiles the 22 core technical stage reports into a publication-grade reference document.

Modern industrial operations generate massive volumes of heterogeneous, unstructured, and non-stationary telemetry. Existing machine learning and agentic approaches fail in production due to silent data destruction, lack of physical constraint enforcement, and non-deterministic model routing. The AI-ConneX platform addresses these failure modes through a contract-first, data-centric architecture. This document specifies: (1) deterministic Compiler and Data Profiler engines for schema normalization; (2) candidate DAG family assignment and recipe orchestration; (3) leakage-safe Feature Engineering and PREPARE quarantine pipelines; (4) the S.T.E.M. model training execution spine; (5) Agentic Studio's Visualizer Ground-State, Agent Builder, immutable Agent SPEC blueprints, and secure Runtime execution plane; and (6) multi-tenant isolation, telemetry governance, and Kubernetes microservice deployment patterns.

Industrial artificial intelligence cannot be built on optimistic assumptions. Unlike web or consumer software, a single false positive or unvalidated model prediction in a chemical plant, power station, or automated manufacturing facility can lead to catastrophic hardware damage, unplanned downtime, or safety compromises. AI-ConneX is engineered around a strict design philosophy: the AI model recommends, the agent proposes, but the deterministic platform validates, compiles, and enforces security boundaries. This Master Specification establishes the technical foundation for trustworthy, resilient, and enterprise-grade industrial automation.

sections.heading_text: Chapter 1: Three Studios Independence and Microservice Modularity
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 1: Three Studios Independence and Microservice Modularity
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

THREE-STUDIO INDEPENDENCE & MICROSERVICE MODULARITY

Data Studio • ML Studio • Agentic StudioArchitecture Proof • Modular Contracts • Deployment Models • POCVersion 1.0 | 14 August 2026

Figure 1.1: AI-ConneX Platform High-Level Overall Architecture Topology

AI-ConneX can be architected as three independently deployable Studios rather than one inseparable application. Independence means each Studio owns a bounded capability, its release lifecycle, APIs, storage boundaries and operational SLOs. Integration happens through explicit contracts—Manifest/Artifact IDs, REST/gRPC APIs, event streams and versioned schemas—not by importing internal code or directly sharing databases.

This is a stronger fit for industrial customers because a factory can consume Data Studio for data organization and visualization without buying ML, consume ML Studio only when predictive modeling is needed, or consume Agentic Studio as an automation/operations layer. The complete AI-ConneX platform remains available when all three are joined.

This architecture follows established cloud-native guidance: loosely coupled components with well-defined responsibilities are easier to scale and change independently. CNCF describes cloud-native software as loosely coupled, resilient, manageable and observable, and notes that microservices handle well-defined tasks. citeturn0search0turn0search10

Independence does not mean zero dependencies. It means dependencies are externalized as stable contracts. A Studio may consume another Studio's artifact/API without becoming structurally dependent on its implementation.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 3. Why This Is Actually Possible
sections.content:
The proof is architectural: each Studio has a distinct bounded context, can expose a network/API boundary, can package its runtime independently, can persist its own state, and can consume immutable artifacts through contracts. The Twelve-Factor methodology explicitly treats backing services as attached resources and separates build, release and run. CNCF's modern interpretation also emphasizes independent components, APIs and automated deployment. citeturn0search1turn0search7

ONNX Runtime strengthens the ML independence claim because an approved model can be packaged as a portable inference artifact and executed across cloud, edge and other hardware environments without requiring the original training framework at serving time. citeturn0search2turn0search8

AI-ConneX Platform│├── DATA STUDIO│   └── Data Intelligence / Organization Boundary│├── ML STUDIO│   └── Model Intelligence / Prediction Boundary│└── AGENTIC STUDIO    └── Automation / Decision-Orchestration BoundaryShared Platform Contracts├── Identity / Tenant├── Manifest & Artifact IDs├── API/Event contracts├── Telemetry├── Policy└── Release / Deployment

The shared layer should contain contracts and platform services, not Studio-specific business logic. This prevents the shared layer from becoming a hidden monolith.

If a customer provides an already-clean, feature-ready dataset satisfying ML Studio's input contract, ML Studio can operate without running Data Studio. If the dataset does not satisfy the contract, Jane can recommend Data Studio; that is a service dependency at the workflow level, not a code dependency.

The serving artifact can be packaged independently. ONNX Runtime supports inference from models originating in multiple frameworks and across cloud, edge and mobile environments. citeturn0search2turn0search3

Translate approved automation intent into an Agent SPEC.

Build/validate agent runtime configuration.

AGENTIC STUDIOAPI Gateway  │  ├── /agent-specs  ├── /agents  ├── /runs  ├── /tools  ├── /knowledge  ├── /visualizer  └── /alertsOwns:  Agent Registry  Tool Registry  Knowledge references  Agent Run Store  Policy bindings  Agent telemetryConsumes:  Industrial data APIs/events  Optional ML inference API  Optional Data Studio data API  User Intent

Agentic Studio therefore does not require ML Studio. It can operate on deterministic rules, data services, APIs and tools. Conversely, when an ML model exists, Agentic Studio can consume it through the model's inference contract.
This matrix is the key commercial proof: AI-ConneX is a platform of composable products, not a forced all-or-nothing suite.
Studios should never integrate by importing one another's private Python modules or querying one another's internal database tables. They integrate through contracts.

sections.heading_text: 10. Manifest as the Universal Join Key
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 10. Manifest as the Universal Join Key
sections.content:

The manifest therefore acts like an industrial passport: it joins the lifecycle while preserving Studio boundaries.
For high-volume or low-latency internal calls, gRPC may be added without changing the domain contracts. REST remains the primary external integration surface for simplicity.

Shared infrastructure is acceptable; shared tables with unrestricted cross-Studio writes are not. Each Studio owns its data model and exposes access through APIs/events.

CNCF guidance emphasizes well-defined services, probes, resource limits, lifecycle management and restricted permissions as important properties for cloud-native deployments. citeturn0search0
Semantic versioning and compatibility rules should be applied to APIs and artifact schemas. A Studio can evolve independently when it preserves its published contract.

Consumers declare the contract version they support.

Provider maintains N and N-1 compatibility for a defined window.

Breaking changes use a new API/schema version.

Adapters translate old contracts where necessary.

Release gates test consumer/provider compatibility.

Manifest references immutable versions.

/v1/data/compile/v2/data/compileschema_version: "1.2"contract_compatibility: ["1.0","1.1","1.2"]
This is the operational meaning of modularity: a failure in one bounded context should not automatically become a platform-wide outage.

Cloud-native architecture benefits from scaling services according to their own workload rather than scaling an entire monolith. CNCF describes service components as individually scalable and operationally manageable. citeturn0search0

Each Studio can have an edge profile. Data Studio may run fully at a plant to organize and visualize data. ML Studio can deploy an ONNX inference service at the edge without shipping the training environment. Agentic Studio can run a constrained local toolkit with approved tools and cached knowledge.

ONNX Runtime supports multiple execution providers and hardware environments, allowing the same model-serving contract to target CPU, GPU and specialized accelerators subject to model/provider compatibility. citeturn0search8

CNCF's edge-native guidance specifically calls out edge autonomy, capability sensitivity, data persistence, metrics/logs and edge operations as distinct design concerns. citeturn0search6

The same services can be deployed in Kubernetes or equivalent cloud infrastructure. The platform layer supplies ingress, identity, secrets, service discovery, autoscaling, observability and release orchestration. The Studios remain application-level services rather than becoming inseparable platform components.

This layered modularity means AI-ConneX can start as a single platform deployment for operational simplicity while retaining the ability to extract each Studio into an independent microservice deployment later.

sections.heading_text: 30. Proof of Concept — Three Independent Deployments
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 30. Proof of Concept — Three Independent Deployments
sections.content:
The strongest POC is not a diagram; it is three separate deployments that are intentionally operated with the other two turned off.

Deploy Data Studio alone with an industrial CSV/Parquet/time-series dataset.

Demonstrate compilation, profiling, DAG, preparation and visualization.

Expose the prepared dataset via its API.

Stop ML Studio and Agentic Studio completely; Data Studio must remain functional.

Deploy ML Studio alone with an externally prepared dataset satisfying the Dataset/Feature Contract.

Train/evaluate, select a model and expose inference.

Stop Data Studio; ML Studio must remain functional.

Deploy Agentic Studio with an external REST/MQTT data source.

Create an agent and run a tool/monitoring workflow.

Stop Data Studio and ML Studio; Agentic Studio must remain functional for capabilities not requiring them.

Connect all three through contracts and demonstrate the enhanced end-to-end workflow.

Change and redeploy only one Studio while the other two remain live.

This modularity directly supports industrial procurement. A plant that only needs data organization and mathematical visualization can purchase/deploy Data Studio as a service. A process engineering group can consume ML Studio's training or inference API. An operations group can consume Agentic Studio for alarms, monitoring and tool orchestration. The enterprise can later join them without replacing the earlier deployments.

It does not mean duplicating identity, policy and telemetry in three incompatible ways.

It does not mean each Studio has a separate user experience with no common Jane experience.

It does not mean arbitrary direct database access.

It does not mean every Studio must ship every dependency.

It does not mean the Studios cannot cooperate.

It means cooperation is explicit, replaceable and contract-driven.

A Studio may depend on another Studio's CONTRACT, but must not depend on another Studio's INTERNAL IMPLEMENTATION.

GOOD:ML Studio → GET /v1/data/{dataset}/feature-contractBAD:ML Studio → SELECT * FROM data_studio.internal_feature_tableGOOD:Agentic Studio → POST /v1/models/{model}/inferBAD:Agentic Studio → import ml_studio.private.training.pipeline
This is an architecture-stage compliance report, not a certification. Production status requires implementation evidence and organization-specific regulatory, cybersecurity and industrial validation.

The Twelve-Factor methodology supports explicit dependencies, configuration separation, backing-service abstraction, build/release/run separation and independently runnable service processes. citeturn0search7turn0search1

CNCF's cloud-native principles describe loosely coupled, observable, manageable services and emphasize lifecycle management, probes, resource controls, permissions and fault-aware deployment. citeturn0search0

CNCF's cloud-native reference architecture explicitly describes applications as distributable and built from loosely coupled services, each performing a single function. citeturn0search10

CNCF edge-native guidance adds autonomy, capability sensitivity, data persistence and edge operations—important when AI-ConneX Studios are independently deployed into plants. citeturn0search6

ONNX Runtime provides a portable inference layer across different source frameworks and hardware/software stacks, supporting cloud, edge and mobile deployment. citeturn0search2turn0search8

sections.heading_text: Chapter 2: Stage Wise Industrial Visualization Experience
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 2: Stage Wise Industrial Visualization Experience
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

STAGE-WISE INDUSTRIAL VISUALIZATION EXPERIENCE

Data Studio • ML Studio • Agentic StudioJane + Progressive Tabs + Telemetry-Gated VisibilityResearch, POC, Industrial Value & Visualization CatalogueVersion 1.0 | 14 August 2026

AI-ConneX should deliberately hide pipeline complexity from industrial users while making the pipeline observable. The user should not have to understand Compiler, Profiler, DAG, recipes, feature pipelines, agent runtimes or model orchestration in order to benefit from them. Instead, Jane is the conversational entry point and each Studio exposes a visual workspace whose tabs progressively unlock as trusted telemetry confirms that a stage has completed.

This is not a 'dashboard for every microservice'. It is a human-understandable digital thread: each tab answers what happened, what was found, why the system made its decision, what evidence supports it, and what is available next. NIST describes visual analytics as analytical reasoning facilitated by interactive visual interfaces and specifically identifies manufacturing benefits including more informed operational decisions, communication across engineering teams, support for less experienced users and multiple lifecycle viewpoints. citeturn0search3

The design principle is: **complexity remains in the backend; evidence becomes visible in the frontend.** Tabs are unlocked by stage telemetry, but unlocking does not mean the user is authorized to perform an operational action. Action permissions remain governed by the platform's tenant, role, policy and approval controls.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 2. Why This Matters to Industrialists
sections.content: NIST's manufacturing visualization research notes that access to data can become overwhelming unless visualization helps humans cognitively integrate information. citeturn0search0

AI-ConneX                       |              +--------+--------+              |                 |             Jane            Studio              |                 |       Intent / explanation   Visual Workspace                                |                   +------------+------------+                   |            |            |               Stage Tabs    Evidence     Telemetry                   |             LOCKED → READY → LIVE                   |             next stage unlocks

The user sees Jane plus the Studio's visual workspace. Internal services remain hidden unless an authorized technical mode is enabled. This keeps the default experience industrialist-friendly.
Telemetry is therefore a state machine, not merely a progress bar.

{  "execution_uid": "EXEC-...",  "tenant_uid": "TEN-...",  "studio": "DATA",  "stage": "PROFILER",  "status": "READY",  "started_at": "...",  "completed_at": "...",  "artifact_refs": ["MANIFEST-..."],  "metrics": {    "rows": 1200000,    "columns": 84,    "quality_score": 0.93  },  "warnings": 3,  "evidence_refs": ["EVID-..."]}

The frontend should unlock a stage only when the backend emits a signed/authorized stage-completion event and the referenced artifact passes validation. Client-side timers must never unlock tabs by themselves.

Overview: what happened?

Explore: what does the data/system look like?

Compare: what changed or differs?

Explain: why did AI/pipeline make this decision?

Evidence: which data/telemetry/recipe/model supports it?

History: what happened across runs/time?

Next: what can the user do now?

Every visualization should answer a defined industrial question. Avoid charts whose only purpose is decoration.

Default UI: Jane + Data Explorer. Jane explains the plan and results in natural language; Data Explorer is the visual workspace. The user does not need to see Compiler, Profiler, DAG or Recipe Orchestrator as separate backend services. They appear as understandable stage tabs.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 7.4 Mathematical/Physics Layer in Data Studio
sections.content:
For datasets where no ML model is required, Data Studio can expose mathematical and physics-derived views: FFT, RMS, variance, rate-of-change, energy proxies, pressure/flow relationships, vibration bands, temperature gradients and domain-specific equations. These are explanatory/analytical layers unless explicitly validated as engineering models.

Vibration → FFT → dominant frequency → possible mechanical signature.

Motor current → RMS/crest factor → load/abnormality indicators.

Pressure + flow → operating envelope visualization.

Temperature → gradient/time derivative → thermal behavior.

Production cycle → cycle-time distribution → bottleneck visualization.

Maintenance logs → text categories + temporal clustering.

NIST has demonstrated visual analytics for heterogeneous machine-maintenance data, including patterns useful for diagnosis and preventive maintenance while retaining a human-in-the-loop. citeturn0search13turn0search8

Industrialists can understand data preparation without learning Python, SQL or ETL.

Plant engineers can visually verify whether a join or merge made sense.

Quality teams can see whether missingness/outliers are concentrated in a machine or period.

Maintenance teams can inspect frequency-domain signatures without requesting a separate analysis.

Managers can understand why the platform recommends ML or a direct data service.

Experienced engineers can use the same visual evidence to validate automated decisions.

Training becomes easier because the system shows the reasoning path rather than only the final artifact.

Default UI: Jane + Model Plots. Jane remains the conversational planning and explanation layer. Model Plots is the mathematical/statistical/physical visualization workspace. The user should see the model-development lifecycle as understandable stages rather than a notebook or ML engineering console.

sections.heading_text: 10. Why Model Plots Matter to Industrialists
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 10. Why Model Plots Matter to Industrialists
sections.content:
An industrial model cannot be judged only by one metric. A model can have acceptable accuracy while violating physical expectations, failing under a specific operating regime, or being too expensive/slow for deployment. The Model Plots workspace therefore combines statistical evidence with physical/domain evidence.

Statistical layer answers: 'Is it predictive?'

Mathematical layer answers: 'How does it behave?'

Physical layer answers: 'Does it make engineering sense?'

Operational layer answers: 'Can it run reliably?'

Business layer answers: 'Is it useful enough to deploy?'

This human-centered approach is consistent with research on digital-twin HMI, where visualization and interaction are used to bridge cyber-physical information and human decision-making. citeturn0search18turn0search2

Default UI: Jane + Agent Studio Visualizer. The visualizer joins the elements of the Agentic Studio rather than exposing users to internal microservices. The user sees the agent's identity, purpose, knowledge, current state, evidence, tools, decisions, actions, alerts and outcomes.

The visualizer must not expose private chain-of-thought. Instead it provides auditable evidence: the user intent, relevant authorized sources, observed telemetry, rules/policies applied, tool calls, approvals, action outcomes and concise reasons. This gives industrialists inspectability without exposing hidden internal reasoning.

USER INTENT   ↓OBSERVED TELEMETRY   ↓AUTHORIZED KNOWLEDGE   ↓POLICY / CONSTRAINT   ↓RECOMMENDATION   ↓APPROVAL (if required)   ↓TOOL ACTION   ↓OBSERVED OUTCOME

The strongest AI-ConneX UX is not three unrelated dashboards. The same execution UID, manifest UID, model UID, agent UID and telemetry lineage should connect the Studios.

DATA STUDIOManifest  ↓ML STUDIOModel  ↓AGENTIC STUDIOAgent  ↓Telemetry  ↓OutcomeCross-links:Dataset → Feature → Model → Agent → Asset → Alert → Outcome

An industrialist should be able to click from a model anomaly to the feature that drove it, then to the source data, then to the affected asset, then to the agent's evidence and action.
The system should not force every user to see every chart. The underlying evidence remains available according to permissions, but the default visual density should match the user's job.

sections.heading_text: 15. Tab Unlocking Across the Three Studios
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 15. Tab Unlocking Across the Three Studios
sections.content: The exact event names are implementation examples. Production contracts should version these events and reject stale or unauthorized events.

One chart = one primary question.

Always show units, time zone and sampling period for industrial signals.

Show data freshness prominently.

Never imply causality from correlation alone.

Show sample size and confidence/uncertainty where applicable.

Allow drill-down from aggregate to source records.

Preserve engineering units and calibration metadata.

Do not hide warnings behind tooltips only.

Separate measured, derived, predicted and simulated values visually and semantically.

Never mix simulation and live telemetry without an explicit label.

Show last successful telemetry timestamp.

Show data quality beside the visualization.

Provide downloadable evidence/report views.

Use consistent asset IDs and terminology across Studios.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 17. Industrial Safety and Trust Rules
sections.content:
Visualization is advisory unless the control path is explicitly authorized.

An alarm visualization must not imply that an alarm has been acknowledged unless an actual acknowledgment exists.

Predicted values must be labeled as predictions.

Physics-derived values must be labeled as calculated/estimated unless validated.

Stale telemetry must be visually distinct from live telemetry.

Agent recommendations must be distinguishable from executed actions.

Action status must be sourced from the tool/industrial system, not inferred by the UI.

All cross-tenant visualization queries must be tenant-authorized.

sections.content:

sections.heading_text: 20. How Beneficial Is This for Industrialists?
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 20. How Beneficial Is This for Industrialists?
sections.content:
The strongest benefit is not prettier dashboards. It is reducing the cognitive cost of understanding an otherwise invisible industrial data/AI pipeline.

NIST's manufacturing visualization work specifically emphasizes the value of visual analytics for operational decision-making, cross-team communication, knowledge transfer and giving less experienced users augmented views. citeturn0search3

NIST's manufacturing visualization survey identified the central challenge that simply giving humans access to large amounts of manufacturing data can overwhelm them; interactive visualization can help integrate information cognitively. citeturn0search0

NIST's Product Lifecycle Data Exploration and Visualization program frames visual analytics as interactive analytical reasoning and targets smart-manufacturing efficiency, agility, communication and knowledge transfer. citeturn0search3

Research on digital-twin HMI in manufacturing shows that visualization is being used to connect cyber-physical systems with human interaction, including lifecycle and high-value information visualization. citeturn0search2turn0search18

Research on visual analytics for machine maintenance demonstrates that high-dimensional, heterogeneous maintenance information benefits from interactive analytical approaches and human-in-the-loop diagnosis. citeturn0search13

Research on digital-twin visualization using AR reports intuitive and continuous visualization of CNC machine data, illustrating how a visual interface can bridge digital information and physical equipment. citeturn0search1

Recent human-centric digital-twin work likewise reports improvements in spatial awareness and decision support through visual interfaces, while emphasizing the need for rigorous usability and scalability validation. citeturn0search11turn0search16

frontend/├── jane/├── shared/│   ├── stage-tabs/│   ├── telemetry-state/│   ├── evidence/│   ├── lineage/│   ├── freshness/│   └── permissions/├── data-explorer/│   ├── ingest/│   ├── profile/│   ├── dag/│   ├── prepare/│   ├── features/│   └── service/├── model-plots/│   ├── split/│   ├── metrics/│   ├── mathematical/│   ├── physical/│   ├── judge/│   └── deployment/└── agent-visualizer/    ├── blueprint/    ├── knowledge/    ├── graph/    ├── telemetry/    ├── runtime/    ├── toolkit/    ├── actions/    └── outcome/

Technology should remain replaceable behind a visualization contract. Industrial deployments may require on-premise/offline operation, so frontend bundles and chart libraries should support controlled/private environments.

Do not use color as the only indication of status.

Support keyboard navigation.

Provide text equivalents for critical status.

Use large, readable status indicators in control-room contexts.

Allow reduced-density views.

Allow engineering units and decimal precision to be configured.

Provide high-contrast mode where required.

Keep alert hierarchy consistent.

Test with actual operators/engineers, not only software developers.

Human-factors research on process-control environments emphasizes the importance of operator-centered design and situation awareness. citeturn0search6turn0search4

USER | vJANE"Tell me what you want to achieve." | +---------------- DATA STUDIO ----------------+ | Data Explorer                               | | [Intent][Ingest][Profile][DAG][Prepare]...  | |        tabs unlock as evidence arrives      | +---------------------------------------------+ | v +---------------- ML STUDIO ------------------+ | Model Plots                                 | | [Readiness][Split][Train][Metrics][Judge]   | | [Math][Physics][Compare][Deploy]            | +---------------------------------------------+ | v +--------------- AGENTIC STUDIO --------------+ | Agent Visualizer                            | | [Blueprint][Knowledge][Graph][Telemetry]    | | [Runtime][Evidence][Toolkit][Actions]...    | +---------------------------------------------+ | vUNDERSTAND → VERIFY → DECIDE → ACT → MEASURE

The industrialist therefore experiences one coherent journey rather than a collection of engineering tools. Jane explains; the visual workspace demonstrates; telemetry unlocks evidence; lineage connects stages; policy controls action.

The proposed visualization layer is strategically important for AI-ConneX because the platform's value is not only that it can automate data engineering, ML and industrial agents. Its value is that an industrialist can understand what the system is doing without becoming a data scientist, ML engineer or agent-runtime specialist.

Data Studio should make the data understandable. ML Studio should make mathematical/model behavior understandable. Agentic Studio should make industrial context, evidence, decisions and actions understandable. The three experiences should be joined by common execution, lineage and telemetry identifiers.

The recommended UX is therefore: **Jane as the conversational guide + stage tabs as the digital thread + telemetry as the unlock mechanism + visualizations as evidence + lineage as the connective tissue + policy as the safety boundary.**

sections.heading_text: Chapter 3: InHouse Metaphorical Agents Catalogue and Architecture
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 3: InHouse Metaphorical Agents Catalogue and Architecture
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

IN-HOUSE AGENT METAPHOR SYSTEM

Metaphorical Agent Catalogue • Metaphor Selector • Validation • Runtime ContractData Studio • ML Studio • Agentic Studio • Cross-Studio ProcessesR&D → Failure Analysis → Architecture → POC → Compliance Report #5Version 1.0 | 14 August 2026

AI-ConneX uses many internal agents. Naming every internal agent only by an engineering function can make the architecture difficult for industrial users to understand. The proposed Metaphorical Agent layer gives each agent a controlled, domain-appropriate metaphor: a familiar role or object that explains its responsibility without pretending that the software is human.

The metaphor is a user-interface and communication device, not an implementation dependency. Internal IDs remain stable technical identifiers; the metaphor is a presentation label stored in a governed registry. This distinction is essential for industrial safety, auditability and localization.

Research supports the idea that metaphors can improve comprehension of unfamiliar interfaces, but also shows that metaphor choice changes perceptions of AI competence, warmth and willingness to collaborate. Therefore AI-ConneX must select metaphors systematically, validate them with target users, and explicitly disclose the underlying technical capability and limitations. citeturn0search2turn0search1

For manufacturing specifically, research on industrial icons and visual analytics indicates that semantic alignment between a visual representation and its underlying industrial entity can improve search efficiency and cognitive performance. citeturn0search12turn0search7

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 2. What a Metaphorical Agent Is
sections.content: Example: the technical agent `dataset_join_validator` may be presented as the **Bridge Inspector** because it checks whether two data structures can be safely connected. The agent does not literally inspect a physical bridge and must not claim physical authority.

Metaphors must explain, never conceal.

One technical responsibility should have one primary metaphor per user context.

Metaphors must be familiar to the target industrial audience.

Prefer industrial/process/object metaphors over exaggerated human personas.

Do not imply human consciousness, emotions, legal authority or independent accountability.

Do not imply physical safety certification unless the agent actually performs a certified function.

Metaphor labels are versioned and governed like product terminology.

Every metaphor has a plain-language explanation available on hover/click.

Metaphors must be consistent across Studios.

Safety-critical actions use explicit technical action labels in addition to metaphors.

Metaphor changes must not change agent behavior.

Interface-metaphor research describes metaphor as presenting a new idea in terms of a familiar one and proposes systematic steps for selecting, implementing and evaluating interface metaphors. It also warns that recognition of the metaphor and its relationship to actual functionality are critical. citeturn0search2

Research on conceptual metaphors in human-AI collaboration found that metaphor framing can influence perceived warmth, competence, usability and willingness to cooperate even when the underlying agent behavior is unchanged. This is a direct reason AI-ConneX needs governance rather than ad-hoc naming. citeturn0search1turn0search4

Research on visual metaphors found that schema congruency and contextual detail can improve comprehension of complex data interfaces. citeturn0search5

Recent work on industrial icons reports that metaphorical object representations can affect cognitive performance, while studies of industrial process icons emphasize semantic-entity relevance and search efficiency. citeturn0search7turn0search12

NIST describes visual analytics as analytical reasoning facilitated by interactive visual interfaces and identifies benefits for manufacturing including operational decision-making, communication across engineering teams, knowledge transfer and support for less experienced users. citeturn0search6

NIST's machine-maintenance research demonstrates coordinated visual analytics for heterogeneous maintenance data and emphasizes human-in-the-loop interpretation. citeturn0search3

These findings support AI-ConneX using metaphors as a thin comprehension layer over evidence-rich visualizations, rather than using metaphors as substitutes for evidence.
The preferred vocabulary is deliberately industrial and functional. Human-role metaphors should not imply that the agent has human judgment or accountability.

AI-ConneX should not ask an LLM to invent a metaphor at runtime and immediately display it. Instead, a governed Metaphor Registry stores approved metaphors. A selector ranks approved candidates and a validator rejects poor matches.

Agent Role   ↓Studio + Process Context   ↓Metaphor Registry   ↓Candidate Ranking   ↓Semantic / Safety Validation   ↓User-context suitability   ↓Approved Metaphor   ↓Jane + UI + Documentation
Weights are starting points for the POC and must be calibrated through user studies.

{  "metaphor_id": "META-DS-COMPILER-001",  "technical_agent": "compiler_agent",  "studio": "DATA",  "role": "format_unification",  "label": "Universal Adapter",  "plain_explanation": "Converts heterogeneous input into the unified data contract.",  "allowed_claims": [    "format normalization",    "schema conversion"  ],  "forbidden_claims": [    "understands the physical process",    "certifies data correctness"  ],  "risk_level": "low",  "locale": "en-IN",  "version": "1.0.0",  "status": "approved"}

Initial assumption: every internal agent needs a memorable metaphor. Finding: too many metaphors increase cognitive load.

Initial assumption: human job titles are easiest. Finding: they can imply authority, competence and accountability that the software does not possess.

Initial assumption: one metaphor works for every audience. Finding: operator, engineer and executive mental models differ.

Initial assumption: metaphor can be generated freely by an LLM. Finding: terminology drift and unsafe claims can occur.

Initial assumption: metaphors can replace technical explanations. Finding: industrial users still need evidence and exact status.

Initial assumption: visual metaphors are universally understood. Finding: cultural and domain context changes comprehension.

Initial assumption: metaphor is cosmetic. Finding: research shows metaphor changes perceptions of AI competence and cooperation.

Jane should introduce a metaphor only when it helps comprehension. The recommended response pattern is: metaphor first, technical identity second, evidence third.

"Think of the Profiler as a Surveyor.It measures the shape and quality of your dataset.Technical stage: Data Profiler.Current status: Ready.Evidence: 84 columns profiled; 3 quality warnings."

This prevents the metaphor from becoming a substitute for technical truth.

sections.heading_text: 27. Metaphors for the Full AI-ConneX Journey
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 27. Metaphors for the Full AI-ConneX Journey
sections.content: The metaphor chain deliberately moves from familiar industrial workflow concepts toward increasingly complex AI concepts. This gives the industrial user a coherent mental model rather than a collection of unrelated agent names.

POC objective: determine whether metaphor labels improve task comprehension without increasing unsafe overtrust.

Recruit representative plant engineers, maintenance personnel, plant managers and data/ML specialists.

Give participants the same AI-ConneX workflow with and without metaphors.

Measure time to identify what each agent does.

Measure error rate when predicting what an agent can and cannot do.

Measure ability to locate evidence and stage status.

Measure perceived competence and trust.

Test high-risk labels such as Gatekeeper, Inspector, Operator and Sentinel.

Test localized versions if required.

Collect confusion points and revise registry.

Freeze only metaphors that pass comprehension and safety thresholds.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 30. Compliance Report #5 — Metaphorical Agent Layer
sections.content: This is a design-stage compliance report, not a certification. Final compliance status requires implementation evidence, testing, risk assessment and applicable regulatory review.

Do not allow a metaphor to grant or imply permissions.

Do not expose hidden tenant information through metaphor selection.

Do not include sensitive plant names, asset IDs or secrets in metaphor metadata.

Keep LLM-generated candidate suggestions separate from approved production vocabulary.

Record who approved a metaphor and when.

Use technical labels in machine-to-machine APIs.

Require explicit confirmation for action-producing agents.

Treat 'Operator', 'Controller', 'Safety Inspector' and similar terms as controlled vocabulary.

Keep a fallback technical label if metaphor service is unavailable.

AI-ConneX should implement a **Metaphorical Agent Registry and Selector as a governed presentation service**, not as a free-form LLM naming feature. The technical agent remains the source of truth. The metaphor is a controlled mental-model aid.

The ideal user experience is:

Jane:"Your Surveyor has finished profiling the data."Technical:Data Profiler — READYEvidence:84 columns • 1.2M rows • 93% quality score • 3 warningsNext:DAG / Family assignment is now available.

This pattern gives industrialists the familiarity of a real-world workflow while preserving the precision, evidence and accountability required by an industrial AI platform.

The Metaphorical Agent layer can become an important part of AI-ConneX's human-centered architecture, provided it remains subordinate to technical truth. The strongest design is not to turn software into fictional employees. It is to give complex technical functions familiar industrial mental models: Adapter, Surveyor, Inspector, Route Map, Workshop, Test Bench, Blueprint, Control Room, Lens and Logbook.

This approach is particularly suitable for AI-ConneX because the platform already uses progressive visualization and Jane as the conversational interface. Metaphors become the connective vocabulary between Jane, stage tabs, visual evidence and internal agents—making a sophisticated multi-agent industrial system easier to learn, navigate and audit.

sections.heading_text: Chapter 4: Data Studio BRAIN Whole Architecture Documentation
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 4: Data Studio BRAIN Whole Architecture Documentation
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

DATA STUDIO — THE BRAIN

Compiler • Data Profiler • DAG Assigner • Recipe Orchestrator

Figure 4.5: Brain Internal Pipeline Handoff Flow

Industrial AI Pipeline Intelligence & Execution Planning — Whole-Stage Technical Documentation

Figure 4.1: Data Studio Master Architecture — Chatbot, The Brain, PREPARE & FE Nodes

sections.heading_text: 1. Executive Definition — Why These Four Are the Brain
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 1. Executive Definition — Why These Four Are the Brain
sections.content:
AI-ConneX Data Studio can be understood as having four cognitive/decision layers between the user's business intent and the eventual AI execution. The Compiler understands and normalizes the physical data. The Data Profiler understands what the data actually contains. The DAG Assigner decides what computational workflows are plausible. The Recipe Orchestrator converts that decision into a concrete, validated execution plan. Together they answer four different questions: Can I understand this data? What is this data? What can I responsibly do with it? Exactly how should I execute it?

Figure 4.2: The Brain Vertical Architecture — Four Internal Cognitive Layers

This architecture is strongly aligned with data-centric AI: recent research emphasizes that improving the data systematically is as important as improving the model, and industrial AI requires data quality, provenance, reproducibility and lifecycle governance. citeturn0search1turn0search9

Figure 4.3: The Brain Cognitive Intelligence Node Block

The Brain is not 'an AI model that predicts something'. It is an intelligence layer that converts industrial ambiguity into a validated computational contract.

INDUSTRIALIST   |   | "I want to predict / detect / optimize X"   vCHATBOT / INTENT   |   v================ DATA STUDIO BRAIN ================   |   +--> COMPILER   |      "What format is this and how do I unify it?"   |   +--> DATA PROFILER   |      "What does this data really look like?"   |   +--> DAG ASSIGNER   |      "What workflows/algorithm families fit?"   |   +--> RECIPE ORCHESTRATOR          "How exactly do we execute it safely?"====================================================   |   vEXECUTION ENGINE   |   vMODEL / ANALYTICS / INDUSTRIAL DECISION

Figure 4.4: User Intent Entry Pathway — JANE Chatbot to The Brain

sections.heading_text: 3. Why This Is Particularly Suitable for Industry
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 3. Why This Is Particularly Suitable for Industry
sections.content:
Industrial environments differ from classroom ML datasets. A factory, utility, plant, logistics operation or process line may have PLC exports, SCADA logs, MES tables, ERP extracts, CSVs, spreadsheets, JSON, database dumps, zipped archives and multiple files with inconsistent schemas. Recent industrial AI literature continues to identify fragmented operational data and weak data foundations as major barriers to scaling AI. citeturn0news35

Industrialists generally care about business outcomes, not data-science plumbing.

They often possess valuable historical data but not a standardized ML-ready representation.

Existing datasets may be generated by multiple machines, software systems, vendors and time periods.

Domain experts understand the process but should not be forced to manually engineer data pipelines.

Industrial systems require traceability: a result should be explainable back to its source data and transformations.

Production environments require repeatability, versioning, controlled changes and failure isolation.

AI-ConneX separates business intent from technical implementation while retaining the connection between them.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 5. Component 1 — Compiler: The Sensory/Translation Cortex
sections.content: The Compiler is the ingestion intelligence. Its purpose is to accept industrial data in whatever practical form the industrial user provides and transform it into a canonical representation that downstream components can reason about.

Detect file and archive types.

Unzip/extract archives when appropriate.

Enumerate files and infer relationships.

Read heterogeneous tabular/structured formats.

Normalize schemas and data types.

Join, append or merge datasets according to explicit evidence and rules.

Preserve source files and source-level lineage.

Produce a canonical data artifact and machine-readable compilation report.

Surface ambiguity instead of silently making unsafe assumptions.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 5.2 Why It Matters to Industrialists
sections.content: The industrialist does not need to know whether the data must become Parquet, whether two CSVs should be appended, or whether two tables should be joined. The Compiler turns 'here is my plant data' into a consistent input contract.
dataset_uidcanonical_artifactschema.jsonsource_inventory.jsonlineage.jsoncompilation_report_1.jsonquality_summarywarningserrors

sections.heading_text: 6. Component 2 — Data Profiler: The Perception Cortex
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 6. Component 2 — Data Profiler: The Perception Cortex
sections.content: The Data Profiler does not merely calculate statistics. It creates a semantic/structural description of the compiled dataset and merges this metadata with user intent from the previous stage. That combined object becomes the canonical manifest-UID.json.

Column types and semantic candidates.

Target candidates and task type.

Missingness and invalid values.

Cardinality and categorical behavior.

Numeric distributions and outliers.

Timestamp presence, ordering and temporal characteristics.

Entity/group identifiers.

Correlations and potential redundancy.

Data imbalance.

Potential target leakage signals.

Dataset scale and resource characteristics.

A model cannot safely be selected without understanding the data it will receive. The Profiler converts hidden dataset characteristics into explicit constraints that the DAG Assigner and Recipe Orchestrator can consume.

manifest-UID.json|+-- intent+-- dataset identity+-- schema+-- semantic profile+-- quality profile+-- temporal profile+-- entity profile+-- target profile+-- constraints+-- provenance+-- profile version

sections.heading_text: 7. Component 3 — DAG Assigner: The Reasoning/Planning Cortex
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 7. Component 3 — DAG Assigner: The Reasoning/Planning Cortex
sections.content: The DAG Assigner uses the Profiler's profile and the user's intent to determine which algorithm families and DAGs are technically and semantically compatible. It is the bridge from 'what the data is' to 'what computational strategies make sense'.

sections.heading_text: 7.1 Why DAG Instead of Only Algorithm Selection?
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 7.1 Why DAG Instead of Only Algorithm Selection?
sections.content:
Industrial problems rarely consist of a model alone.

A complete solution requires ingestion/preparation, feature creation, splitting, training, evaluation and often post-processing.

Different data structures require different dependency graphs.

Time-series data requires different sequencing from IID tabular data.

Multi-source data may require joins before features.

Some workflows can run in parallel; others cannot.

A DAG provides an explicit dependency and execution structure.
family_idsecondary_family_idsdag_iddag_versioncandidate_scorehard_constraintssoft_constraintsspecial_handlingreasoning/evidenceregistry_version

sections.heading_text: 8. Component 4 — Recipe Orchestrator: The Motor-Control Cortex
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 8. Component 4 — Recipe Orchestrator: The Motor-Control Cortex
sections.content:
The Recipe Orchestrator takes the selected DAG and pulls controlled implementation recipes for PREPARE, FE and STEM. It binds those recipes to the manifest and constructs the executable plan.

DAG:  "Use classification workflow with temporal handling"RECIPE ORCHESTRATOR:  PREPARE:    schema validation    missing-value policy    timestamp normalization  FE:    lag features    rolling features    categorical encoding  STEM:    chronological split    training    evaluation metricsOUTPUT:  recipe_plan.json  manifest binding  lineage  validation evidence

Research on automated data preparation highlights that real-world raw datasets are heterogeneous and that preparation is often a major part of ML work. citeturn0search3turn0search12

sections.heading_text: 9. Why the Four Must Exist Together
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 9. Why the Four Must Exist Together
sections.content: The components therefore form a chain of evidence. Each stage reduces uncertainty for the next stage.

sections.heading_text: 14. Agent Role — Why AI-ConneX Is Not 'Just an Agent'
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 14. Agent Role — Why AI-ConneX Is Not 'Just an Agent'
sections.content:
An agent can assist the four components, but it should not be the source of truth. The architecture is deliberately hybrid: agents can interpret intent, propose mappings and help resolve ambiguity, while deterministic registries, schemas, validators and lineage systems control what can actually execute.

AGENT  |  +--> suggestion  +--> explanation  +--> ambiguity detection  +--> recipe recommendation  |  vVALIDATORS / REGISTRIES  |  +--> PASS --> execution plan  |  +--> FAIL --> human/agent clarification

This is important for industry because unconstrained generation is difficult to audit and reproduce. Provenance-based research similarly emphasizes the importance of screening ML data-preparation pipelines for correctness and leakage. citeturn0search7

sections.heading_text: 20. Why This Is Better Than Traditional Manual ML

sections.content: This does not eliminate expert engineering. It moves expert effort toward domain decisions, constraints, validation and exceptional cases rather than repetitive data plumbing.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 21. Fit for SMEs and Industrialists
sections.content:
Research on data-centric AI for SMEs specifically identifies small datasets, drift and limited ML knowledge as barriers to AI adoption and presents data-centric development as a way to make AI more accessible in industrial settings. citeturn0search11

Lower requirement for specialized ML/data-engineering staff.

Faster first proof of concept.

Reusable recipes reduce repeated engineering cost.

Existing industrial data can be used without first manually converting everything.

Domain experts can specify intent and constraints in business language.

Technical artifacts remain available for engineering teams when deeper control is required.

Central recipe and DAG registries support standardization across plants.

Manifest-based lineage supports audit and incident investigation.

Versioned artifacts enable controlled model lifecycle.

Multiple data sources can be normalized into common contracts.

Policy gates can enforce security and quality standards.

Distributed execution can be introduced without changing the conceptual Brain.

The POC should prove the architecture, not merely demonstrate model accuracy. A successful POC must show that the same Brain can accept different data organizations, infer the relevant profile, assign different DAGs and generate different recipes while preserving lineage.

At least five heterogeneous industrial-style inputs successfully compile.

Compiler preserves source lineage and generates Report #1.

Profiler generates a complete manifest with profile evidence.

DAG Assigner produces at least one valid registry-backed DAG.

Recipe Orchestrator composes PREPARE, FE and STEM stages.

Known leakage scenarios are blocked.

Known invalid joins are blocked or quarantined.

Every artifact is traceable to the manifest UID.

Repeated runs produce reproducible plan artifacts.

Industrial user can understand the generated plan without reading implementation code.

The Brain should be positioned as a constrained, data-centric, provenance-aware pipeline intelligence layer rather than simply another AutoML system. Existing AutoML research has demonstrated automation across preprocessing, feature engineering, model generation and evaluation, but the industrial opportunity is to combine those capabilities with explicit dataset compilation, profile-driven decision making, registry-grounded DAG assignment and auditable execution contracts. citeturn0search0turn0search2

Research on automated data preparation also notes that preparation is often neglected relative to model selection even though real-world raw datasets are heterogeneous and require substantial preparation. This directly supports AI-ConneX's decision to make Compiler, Profiler and Recipe Orchestrator first-class components. citeturn0search3turn0search12

A four-stage Brain abstraction that separates data unification, data understanding, workflow assignment and executable recipe composition.

Manifest-centered handoff between stages.

Industrial-format agnostic compilation before ML reasoning.

Profile-driven DAG assignment instead of model-only selection.

Registry-grounded recipe composition instead of unrestricted generated code.

Intent + data + operational constraints jointly influence execution planning.

Lineage and compliance evidence generated as part of the pipeline rather than after deployment.

sections.content:
It does not blindly clean every dataset.

It does not assume every CSV should be merged.

sections.heading_text: 39. The Industrial Advantage in One Sentence
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 39. The Industrial Advantage in One Sentence
sections.content: AI-ConneX gives an industrialist a path from **'I have messy operational data and a business problem'** to **'I have a validated, traceable and reproducible AI execution plan'** without requiring the industrialist to personally understand every data-engineering, ML-selection and pipeline-orchestration detail.

sections.heading_text: 40. Final Justification — Why These Four Deserve the Name 'Brain'
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 40. Final Justification — Why These Four Deserve the Name 'Brain'
sections.content:
Together, the four components exhibit the functional pattern of a decision system: perception → understanding → reasoning → action planning. The analogy is architectural, not biological. Their value comes from the contracts between them, not from any single component.

Most importantly, they create a boundary between the industrialist and the complexity of AI engineering. The industrialist supplies the problem, context and constraints; the Brain converts those inputs into structured, validated computational decisions; the execution layer performs only what the Brain has authorized.

INDUSTRIALIST                         |                  Business Objective                         |                         v                     CHATBOT                         |                    User Intent                         |                         v                +================+                |   AI-ConneX    |                |     BRAIN      |                +================+                         |             +-----------+-----------+             |           |           |             v           v           v         COMPILER    PROFILER      DAG             |           |        ASSIGNER             |           |           |             +-----------+-----------+                         |                         v                 RECIPE ORCHESTRATOR                         |                  PREPARE → FE → STEM                         |                         v                  VALIDATED PLAN                         |                         v                    EXECUTION                         |              +----------+----------+              |          |          |            MODEL      METRICS    LINEAGE              |          |          |              +----------+----------+                         |                         v                 INDUSTRIAL VALUE

For research publication, position the Brain as a systems architecture and evaluate it experimentally against manual pipeline construction and conventional AutoML baselines. For IP, focus on the specific mechanisms that are actually novel in implementation—particularly the contracts and decision flow between compilation, profiling, DAG assignment, recipe composition, manifest binding and industrial constraints. Novelty should be established through a formal prior-art/patent search before making any patentability claim.

The strongest empirical story is not simply 'AI-ConneX gets higher accuracy'. It is: AI-ConneX reduces time-to-valid-pipeline, reduces invalid/unsafe transformations, improves lineage completeness and reproducibility, and enables industrial users to operationalize heterogeneous data with less specialist intervention.

The Compiler, Data Profiler, DAG Assigner and Recipe Orchestrator are appropriately described as the Brain of AI-ConneX Data Studio because they collectively transform unstructured industrial reality into a controlled computational plan. The Compiler creates a common language for data. The Profiler creates a factual understanding of that data. The DAG Assigner turns facts and intent into a computational strategy. The Recipe Orchestrator turns that strategy into an executable, versioned and auditable plan.

This architecture is particularly suited to industrial AI because it addresses the problem that exists before model selection: industrial data is heterogeneous, contextual, continuously changing and operationally constrained. Research on data-centric AI, automated data preparation, provenance and industrial MLOps supports making data quality, preparation, lineage and reproducibility first-class concerns rather than treating them as incidental preprocessing. citeturn0search1turn0search7turn0search11

Industrial Data Ingestion, Understanding, Unification and Compilation Engine

Project: AI-ConneXPlatform: Industrial AI Solutions PlatformModule: Data StudioComponent: CompilerDocument: Technical R&D and Stage-1 Engineering DocumentationStage: Chatbot → Data Studio Compiler → Data ProfilerDocument Version: 1.0Date: 14 August 2026Status: Architecture / R&D Baseline

Figure 5.1: AI-ConneX Data Studio Compiler Stage Icon

The AI-ConneX Data Studio Compiler is the first machine-processing layer after the AI-ConneX conversational interface.

Its purpose is to eliminate one of the largest barriers between industrial data and artificial intelligence:

Industrial users should not have to understand data engineering, file formats, schemas, joins, merges, encoding, or data normalization before using AI-ConneX.

Industrial data is rarely delivered in a clean, standardized form.

A plant may provide:

CSV files

Excel workbooks

JSON

XML

Parquet

TXT/log files

database exports

ZIP archives

multiple files from multiple machines

historical files

files with different column names

files with different timestamps

files containing different units

datasets containing overlapping records

datasets that need to be appended

datasets that need to be joined

datasets that need to be merged

datasets containing metadata and operational measurements together

The Compiler receives this heterogeneous input and converts it into a validated AI-ConneX Unified Industrial Dataset representation.

The Compiler does not simply convert:

Excel → CSV

or:

ZIP → extracted files

Instead, it performs:

INGEST   ↓IDENTIFY   ↓INSPECT   ↓PROFILE PRE-CHECK   ↓UNDERSTAND   ↓PLAN   ↓UNZIP / EXTRACT   ↓NORMALIZE   ↓JOIN / APPEND / MERGE   ↓SCHEMA HARMONIZATION   ↓TYPE / TIME / UNIT ALIGNMENT   ↓VALIDATION   ↓PROVENANCE   ↓UNIFIED DATASET   ↓DATA PROFILER

The Compiler is assisted by an Agent Helper.

The Agent Helper does not directly manipulate production data without controls.

Its primary responsibility is:

Understand ambiguous industrial datasets and recommend the correct transformation plan.

The Compiler then validates and executes the plan deterministically.

Therefore the architecture follows:

Agent reasons     ↓Compiler validates     ↓Compiler executes     ↓Validator verifies     ↓Profiler receives result

This separation is fundamental to the reliability of AI-ConneX.

sections.heading_text: 2. Position of the Compiler in AI-ConneX
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 2. Position of the Compiler in AI-ConneX
sections.content:
The relevant section of the AI-ConneX architecture is:

JANE / CHATBOT                              │                              │                              ▼                    ┌───────────────────┐                    │   DATA STUDIO     │                    │                   │                    │     COMPILER      │                    └─────────┬─────────┘                              │                    Unified Industrial                         Dataset                              │                              ▼                    ┌───────────────────┐                    │   DATA PROFILER   │                    └─────────┬─────────┘                              │                              ▼                    Recipe Orchestrator                              │                              ▼                        DAG Assigner

Figure 5.2: Ingestion Handshake — Data Studio Compiler to Data Profiler

The Compiler is therefore the boundary between human/industrial intent and structured machine-readable data.

Without AI-ConneX:

Industrialist      ↓Finds data      ↓Calls data engineer      ↓Converts Excel      ↓Unzips files      ↓Checks schemas      ↓Renames columns      ↓Writes Python/Pandas code      ↓Joins datasets      ↓Fixes timestamps      ↓Handles missing values      ↓Exports clean dataset      ↓ML engineer receives dataset

This creates several problems.

Problem 1 — Skill barrier

Industrial personnel may understand:

machines

production

maintenance

process parameters

plant operations

but may not understand:

Python

Pandas

SQL

schemas

ETL

joins

data types

encodings

Problem 2 — Format barrier

Industrial data can arrive in arbitrary formats.

Problem 3 — Schema barrier

Two datasets may represent the same concept using different names.

Example:

Machine_IDmachine_idmachineasset_idequipment_no

Problem 4 — Relationship barrier

The system must determine whether datasets should be:

APPENDEDJOINEDMERGEDLEFT JOINEDAS-OF JOINEDUNIONED

Problem 5 — Time barrier

Industrial datasets frequently contain:

UTC

local time

date only

timestamp

epoch time

different timestamp resolutions

Problem 6 — Unit barrier

For example:

temperature = °Ctemperature = °Fpressure = barpressure = psi

A simple schema match is insufficient.

The Compiler has six primary objectives.

Objective 1 — Format independence

Accept heterogeneous industrial file formats.

Objective 2 — Dataset understanding

Determine what each file/dataset contains.

Objective 3 — Intelligent composition

Determine whether datasets should be:

appended

joined

merged

left/right/full joined

time-aligned

unioned

Objective 4 — Unified representation

Convert the resulting dataset into the AI-ConneX canonical representation.

Objective 5 — Validation

Prevent incorrect transformations from silently entering ML pipelines.

Objective 6 — Provenance

Maintain the lineage of every important transformation.

The AI-ConneX Compiler can be formally defined as:

A schema-aware, provenance-preserving industrial data compilation engine that transforms heterogeneous user-provided datasets into a validated canonical representation suitable for downstream data profiling, feature engineering and machine-learning workflows.

It is therefore an ETL/ELT + schema inference + data reasoning + validation engine.

The most important rule is:

LLM / Agent ≠ Data Executor

The Agent Helper should not be trusted to arbitrarily execute transformations.

Instead:

User Intent    ↓Agent Helper    ↓Transformation Proposal    ↓Compiler Validation    ↓Deterministic Executor    ↓Validation    ↓Output

This protects industrial data from uncontrolled agent behavior.

The R&D process should be divided into the following phases.

R&D-01 — Input Diversity Study

Determine the formats that industrial users are likely to provide.

Initial target

CSVXLSXXLSMJSONXMLTXTLOGPARQUETZIP

Future

PDF tablesAvroORCSQLiteSQL dumpsAPI responsesS3 objectsindustrial databasesOPC-UA exportsMQTT data snapshotsSCADA exportsMES exportsERP exports

The system should never trust the filename extension alone.

For example:

machine.csv

may actually contain:

semicolon-separated data

or:

UTF-16 encoded data

or even malformed binary content.

The Compiler therefore performs:

filename inspection+MIME detection+magic-byte detection+parser probing

The detected type is stored separately from the supplied filename.

ZIP files are particularly important because industrialists frequently send:

plant_data.zip

rather than individual files.

The Compiler therefore needs:

ZIP detection     ↓safe extraction     ↓recursive file discovery     ↓file classification     ↓dataset grouping

A naive implementation might execute:

zipfile.extractall(output_directory)

without checking archive paths.

This can create a Zip Slip/path traversal vulnerability.

A malicious archive could contain:

../../some_sensitive_file

The Compiler must therefore resolve every archive member and verify that the final extraction path remains inside the designated workspace.

Another failure is a compressed archive that is tiny but expands to enormous size.

Example:

Input ZIP:50 MBExpanded:500 GB

Without controls, the server could run out of:

disk

RAM

CPU

worker capacity

The Compiler must implement:

maximum archive sizemaximum uncompressed sizemaximum file countmaximum nesting depthmaximum individual file size

After files are identified, the Compiler creates a discovery report.

Example:

{  "dataset_id": "DS-000184",  "file": "machine_data.csv",  "format": "csv",  "encoding": "utf-8",  "delimiter": ",",  "rows_estimate": 1845023,  "columns": 17,  "has_header": true,  "timestamp_candidates": [    "timestamp",    "event_time"  ],  "identifier_candidates": [    "machine_id"  ]}

This is not yet the final Data Profiler output.

It is a Compiler discovery artifact.

Suppose the user gives:

File A

machine_idtimestamptemperaturepressure

File B

MachineTimeTempPressure

A naive system sees different schemas.

AI-ConneX must infer:

machine_id ←→ Machinetimestamp  ←→ Timetemperature ←→ Temppressure ←→ Pressure

The Agent Helper assists in this process.

Schema matching should use multiple signals.

Schema Match                         │        ┌────────────────┼─────────────────┐        ▼                ▼                 ▼     Name           Data Type          Values   Similarity        Similarity        Similarity        │                │                 │        └────────────────┼─────────────────┘                         ▼                  Semantic Score

Potential scoring:

column_name_similarity+datatype_similarity+sample_value_similarity+unit_similarity+semantic_embedding_similarity+timestamp compatibility+domain vocabulary

The final result should be a confidence score.

The Agent Helper is the intelligent reasoning component.

It receives:

dataset metadata+schemas+sample values+column statistics+user objective+known industrial vocabulary

It produces:

transformation proposal+confidence+reason+required keys+warnings

Example:

{  "operation": "JOIN",  "left": "machine_data",  "right": "production_data",  "keys": [    "machine_id",    "timestamp"  ],  "join_type": "LEFT",  "confidence": 0.94,  "reason": "Both datasets share machine identifier and compatible timestamps."}

The Compiler should prefer APPEND when:

schemas are substantially compatibleANDrecords represent different partitions/time periodsANDno complementary-key relationship is required

Example:

Jan.csvFeb.csvMar.csv

becomes:

Jan +Feb +Mar ↓APPEND

JOIN is appropriate when datasets contain complementary attributes.

Example:

Machine:machine_id | timestamp | temperatureProduction:machine_id | timestamp | production_rate

Output:

machine_idtimestamptemperatureproduction_rate

MERGE should be used when overlapping datasets require reconciliation.

For example:

Machine A:machine_id | temperature | pressureMachine B:machine_id | temperature | vibration

The Compiler may produce:

machine_idtemperaturepressurevibration

But if both datasets contain different values for the same field, the conflict must be recorded rather than silently overwritten.

A major R&D failure mode is an incorrect join.

Example:

Dataset A:

machine_id = M01

appears 100,000 times.

Dataset B:

machine_id = M01

appears 50,000 times.

Joining only on:

machine_id

can potentially create billions of combinations.

This is a many-to-many join explosion.

The Compiler should therefore estimate join cardinality before execution.

Expected join size        ↓Risk estimation        ↓If excessive        ↓Reject / require confirmation

Industrial data may contain:

2026-08-14 10:00:00

while another dataset contains:

14/08/2026 10:00

and another:

1723636200

The Compiler should normalize these into a canonical timestamp representation.

Recommended internal representation:

UTC timestamp+original timezone+original timestamp

Do not discard the original value.

Consider:

Sensor:1-second intervals

and:

Production:1-hour intervals

A normal equality join will fail.

The Compiler should detect granularity differences and potentially recommend:

AS-OF JOINWINDOW JOINRESAMPLINGAGGREGATION

rather than forcing equality.

Example:

Dataset A:temperature = °CDataset B:temperature = °F

The column names are identical.

A purely schema-based Compiler would incorrectly treat them as identical.

Therefore the Compiler must consider:

semantic meaning+unit+value distribution

before combining them.

Industrial files may use:

UTF-8UTF-8 BOMUTF-16Latin-1Windows-1252

The Compiler should attempt safe encoding detection and record:

original_encodingdetected_encodingconversion_applied

CSV is deceptively difficult.

Potential problems:

,;|\t

Different delimiters may be used.

Fields may contain:

"Machine, Line 1"

without being correctly escaped.

The Compiler should detect:

delimiterquote characterescape characterheaderencodingline ending

before parsing.

Industrial Excel workbooks may contain:

multiple sheets

hidden sheets

merged cells

header rows beginning at row 5

notes above the table

multiple tables on one sheet

formulas

macros

blank rows

inconsistent columns

The Compiler therefore needs an Excel discovery stage:

Workbook   ↓Sheet discovery   ↓Table-region detection   ↓Header detection   ↓Schema extraction

JSON can represent:

array of objects

or:

nested objects

or:

deeply nested telemetry

Example:

{  "machine": {    "id": "M01",    "telemetry": {      "temperature": 72.4    }  }}

The Compiler needs a controlled flattening strategy.

It must not arbitrarily flatten every nested structure because hierarchy can contain meaning.

Industrial systems frequently exchange XML-like structured data.

Potential problems:

namespaces

deeply nested structures

malformed XML

external entity attacks

enormous XML expansion

The parser should therefore use secure XML parsing practices.

A column may contain:

123N/A4

The parser may infer it as:

string

instead of:

integer

The Compiler should perform type inference with explicit handling of:

nullmissingNAN/Aunknown-error

Two files may contain overlapping records.

Example:

January.csvJanuary_backup.csv

Appending both creates duplicate records.

The Compiler should calculate duplicate signatures using candidate keys such as:

machine_id+timestamp+measurement

where appropriate.

It should distinguish:

exact duplicate

from:

legitimate repeated observation

Industrial systems evolve.

Version 1:

temperaturepressure

Version 2:

temperaturepressurevibration

Version 3:

temp_cpressure_barvibration_mm_s

The Compiler should not treat this as an error automatically.

It should detect:

schema version change

and create a harmonization plan.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 33. How AI-ConneX Overcomes Agent Errors
sections.content:
The Agent Helper must never be the final authority.

Architecture:

AGENT HELPER                     │                     ▼             Proposed Plan                     │                     ▼              PLAN VALIDATOR                     │        ┌────────────┼─────────────┐        ▼            ▼             ▼     Schema       Cardinality     Units     Check          Check         Check        │            │             │        └────────────┼─────────────┘                     ▼              EXECUTION ENGINE                     │                     ▼              RESULT VALIDATOR

This provides a safety boundary around the LLM.

Recommended policy:

Confidence >= 0.90    → automatic execution0.75–0.89    → execution with warning / optional confirmation0.50–0.74    → ask user or perform additional analysis< 0.50    → do not execute

For high-risk transformations, confidence alone should not be enough.

Example:

Potential many-to-many JOIN

should require explicit validation even if the Agent reports high confidence.

The Compiler should transform the Agent’s recommendation into a deterministic recipe.

Example:

{  "recipe_version": "1.0",  "operations": [    {      "id": "op01",      "type": "UNZIP",      "input": "upload_001"    },    {      "id": "op02",      "type": "APPEND",      "inputs": [        "machine_01.csv",        "machine_02.csv"      ]    },    {      "id": "op03",      "type": "JOIN",      "left": "op02",      "right": "production.xlsx",      "keys": [        "machine_id",        "timestamp"      ],      "join_type": "LEFT"    }  ]}

The recipe becomes the executable specification.

The Recipe Orchestrator converts the recipe into a DAG.

upload_001                  │                UNZIP                  │       ┌──────────┼──────────┐       ▼          ▼          ▼   machine01  machine02  production       │          │          │       └────┬─────┘          │            ▼                │          APPEND             │            │                │            └───────┬────────┘                    ▼                   JOIN                    │                    ▼              NORMALIZATION                    │                    ▼              VALIDATION

This makes the Compiler compatible with the existing Data Studio DAG architecture.

The Compiler should produce a canonical representation rather than merely a CSV.

Recommended structure:

AI-ConneX Unified Industrial Dataset│├── Dataset Metadata│├── Entity Information│├── Timestamp│├── Measurements│├── Events│├── Operational Variables│├── Labels / Targets│├── Units│├── Data Quality│└── Provenance

Every compiled dataset should have metadata similar to:

{  "dataset_id": "ACX-DS-000001",  "source_count": 7,  "compiled_at": "2026-08-14T10:30:00Z",  "schema_version": "1.0",  "row_count": 1845023,  "column_count": 27,  "operations": [    "UNZIP",    "APPEND",    "JOIN",    "NORMALIZE"  ],  "quality_status": "PASS"}

Every transformation should create lineage.

Source File    ↓Source Dataset    ↓Operation    ↓Intermediate Dataset    ↓Operation    ↓Unified Dataset

Example:

{  "operation_id": "OP-00042",  "operation": "JOIN",  "inputs": [    "machine_data.csv",    "production.xlsx"  ],  "keys": [    "machine_id",    "timestamp"  ],  "output": "dataset_stage_03"}

The Compiler should not have only:

SUCCESSFAILURE

Recommended states:

RECEIVEDINSPECTINGWAITING_FOR_AGENTPLAN_READYVALIDATINGEXECUTINGVALIDATING_OUTPUTCOMPILEDWARNINGNEEDS_CONFIRMATIONQUARANTINEDFAILED

Recommended backend

Language:Python 3.13.14API:FastAPI 0.141.1Validation:Pydantic 2.13.1Data processing:Polars 1.43.0SQL / analytical execution:DuckDB 1.5.5Columnar format:Apache Arrow / PyArrow 25.0.0Excel:openpyxl 3.1.5HTTP multipart:python-multipart 0.0.32Environment/package manager:uv 0.11.33Container:DockerTesting:pytestStatic analysis:RuffType checking:mypy or pyrightStructured logging:structlog / standard loggingAgent orchestration:LangGraph or an equivalent internal state-machine layerObject storage:S3-compatible storageMetadata database:PostgreSQLCache:RedisObservability:OpenTelemetry + Prometheus-compatible metrics

The versions should be locked in the project lockfile rather than allowing floating production dependencies.

Polars is recommended for the primary dataframe engine because the Compiler is expected to process potentially large industrial datasets.

Its columnar execution model is well suited to:

filtering

projection

joins

aggregations

transformations

lazy execution

For extremely large datasets, the Compiler should avoid loading the entire dataset into RAM unnecessarily.

DuckDB becomes the SQL execution layer.

It is particularly useful for:

CSVParquetArrowlarge local datasetsjoinsaggregationsSQL transformations

It can complement Polars rather than replacing it.

Recommended division:

Polars→ dataframe transformationsDuckDB→ analytical SQL / large joins / file queryingPyArrow→ columnar interchange

FastAPI exposes Compiler functionality to:

Chatbot

Data Studio UI

internal orchestration

future external integrations

It also provides OpenAPI-based API documentation.

Pydantic should define the contracts between:

Chatbot → CompilerCompiler → Agent HelperAgent Helper → CompilerCompiler → Profiler

This prevents loosely structured JSON from moving between components.

The Agent Helper should ideally operate as a bounded state machine:

DISCOVER   ↓UNDERSTAND   ↓PROPOSE   ↓VALIDATE   ↓REVISE   ↓FINALIZE

This is safer than an unconstrained autonomous agent.

Development machine

Minimum:

CPU:4 coresRAM:16 GBStorage:100 GB free SSDOS:Ubuntu 24.04 / Windows 11 / equivalentPython:3.13.xNetwork:Internet for package/model/API access

Recommended:

CPU:8+ coresRAM:32 GBSSD:500 GB+Network:1 Gbps

For a small industrial deployment:

8 vCPU32 GB RAM500 GB SSD

For larger workloads:

16–32 vCPU64–128 GB RAMNVMe SSDobject storagePostgreSQLRedis

The Compiler should be horizontally scalable because ingestion jobs can be asynchronous.

The Compiler itself does not fundamentally require a GPU.

The Agent Helper may use:

cloud LLM

or:

local LLM

depending on deployment.

Therefore:

Compiler:CPU-firstAgent Helper:CPU / GPU / cloud dependent

This is important for industrial edge deployments.

Example:

APP_ENV=developmentCOMPILER_MAX_UPLOAD_GB=20COMPILER_MAX_ARCHIVE_GB=20COMPILER_MAX_UNCOMPRESSED_GB=100COMPILER_MAX_FILES=10000COMPILER_MAX_ARCHIVE_DEPTH=5WORKSPACE_ROOT=/data/aiconnex/workspacesOBJECT_STORE_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:9000OBJECT_STORE_BUCKET=aiconnex-dataPOSTGRES_URL=postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/aiconnexREDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379/0AGENT_HELPER_MODE=hybridAGENT_CONFIDENCE_AUTO=0.90AGENT_CONFIDENCE_CONFIRM=0.75DEFAULT_TIMEZONE=UTCMAX_JOIN_EXPANSION_FACTOR=10ENABLE_PROVENANCE=trueENABLE_AUDIT_LOG=true

Secrets should never be committed into Git.

The Chatbot should not send an arbitrary natural-language string only.
