sections.heading_text: 58. What the Compiler Receives From Chatbot
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 58. What the Compiler Receives From Chatbot
sections.content: The Compiler receives five conceptual inputs:

sections.heading_text: 1. User Intent2. Data Assets3. Industrial Context4. Constraints5. Expected Objective
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 1. User Intent2. Data Assets3. Industrial Context4. Constraints5. Expected Objective
sections.content:
Example:

User:"Use these files to prepare a dataset for predictive maintenance."Compiler receives:Intent:predictive maintenance preparationAssets:machine_data.zipmaintenance.xlsxsensor.csvDomain:manufacturingConstraints:preserve original datamaintain lineage

The Compiler gives the Agent Helper a controlled discovery package.

{  "job_id": "JOB-001",  "assets": [    {      "asset_id": "A001",      "format": "csv",      "rows": 120000,      "columns": [        {          "name": "Machine_ID",          "dtype": "string"        },        {          "name": "Time",          "dtype": "datetime"        },        {          "name": "Temp",          "dtype": "float"        }      ]    }  ]}

The Agent does not need the entire raw dataset.

It should generally receive:

metadata+schema+statistics+small representative samples

This reduces data leakage and LLM cost.

This is the second most important interface.

The Compiler does not simply send:

clean.csv

to the Data Profiler.

It should send:

UNIFIED DATASET+CANONICAL SCHEMA+DATASET METADATA+QUALITY REPORT+PROVENANCE+TRANSFORMATION RECIPE+STATISTICS

sections.heading_text: 63. What Data Profiler Should NOT Need to Do
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 63. What Data Profiler Should NOT Need to Do
sections.content:
The Data Profiler should not have to figure out:

Is this ZIP?Should these files be joined?Should these files be appended?What is the correct encoding?What was the original file?Which timestamp is equivalent?

That is the Compiler’s responsibility.

The Profiler should begin with:

What is the statistical and structural quality of this already-unified dataset?

This creates clean separation of responsibilities.

For internal processing, the recommended primary output is:

Parquet

rather than CSV.

Why:

columnarcompressedtypedefficientlarge-data friendlyArrow compatibleDuckDB compatiblePolars compatible

CSV can still be offered as an export option.

The Compiler should produce:

dataset.parquetschema.jsonmetadata.jsonrecipe.jsonlineage.jsonquality_report.jsoncompiler_report.json

Optional:

preview.csvsample.parquethuman_readable_report.html

incoming/    ↓quarantine/    ↓extracted/    ↓discovered/    ↓intermediate/    ↓unified/    ↓profiler/

Original input must be preserved separately.

If one file is corrupt:

machine_01.csv  ✓machine_02.csv  ✓machine_03.csv  ✗machine_04.csv  ✓

the entire job should not necessarily crash.

The Compiler can report:

3 files processed1 file quarantined

and either:

continue

or:

request confirmation

depending on the user’s objective.

Bad or suspicious inputs should move to:

data/quarantine/

with:

reasontimestamphashoriginal locationsecurity scan resultparser errorjob ID

Example:

{  "asset_id": "A004",  "status": "QUARANTINED",  "reason": "Malformed XLSX archive",  "sha256": "...",  "job_id": "JOB-001"}

Example:

compiler:  output_format: parquet  preserve_original: true  enable_provenance: truesecurity:  max_upload_gb: 20  max_archive_gb: 20  max_uncompressed_gb: 100  max_files: 10000  max_archive_depth: 5join:  max_expansion_factor: 10  require_key_validation: true  allow_many_to_many: falseagent:  auto_execute_threshold: 0.90  confirmation_threshold: 0.75  max_retries: 3time:  canonical_timezone: UTCstorage:  intermediate_format: parquet

The Compiler should avoid:

df = read_everything_into_memory()

for large industrial datasets.

Instead use:

lazy executionstreamingchunked ingestioncolumn projectionpredicate pushdownParquetDuckDBPolars

Large files should be processed incrementally where possible.

Dataset fingerprints should be calculated.

Example:

SHA-256(file)

If the same file is submitted again:

same hash+same compiler version+same configuration

the Compiler may reuse an existing compiled artifact.

This reduces unnecessary processing.

Every compilation should record:

compiler versionrecipe versionschema versionconfiguration versioninput hashesagent plan versionparser versionsexecution timestamp

Therefore:

Same input+same recipe+same Compiler version+same configuration

should produce reproducible results wherever deterministic execution is possible.

The Compiler is exposed to arbitrary industrial uploads, so it must be treated as an untrusted-input processing service.

Required controls:

authenticationauthorizationfile-size limitsarchive limitspath traversal protectionmalware scanningsandboxed parsingresource limitstimeout limitsnetwork isolationaudit loggingencryptionsecure temporary storagesecret management

AI-ConneX should design the Compiler around controls that can support:

ISO/IEC 27001IEC 62443ISO 9001ISO/IEC 27701India DPDP ActGDPR where applicable

However:

Designing for these controls is not the same as being certified or legally compliant.

Formal compliance requires organizational policies, audits, evidence, risk assessments and certification/legal review.

For industrial environments, IEC 62443 should be treated as particularly important because AI-ConneX may eventually interact with:

OT networksSCADAPLC environmentsMESindustrial machinesedge devices

The Compiler itself should preferably remain separated from direct machine-control paths.

Recommended architecture:

OT Network     │     │ controlled gateway     ▼AI-ConneX ingestion boundary     │     ▼Compiler

The Compiler should not directly issue machine-control commands.

Recommended:

TLS in transitAES-256 or equivalent encryption at restRBACtenant isolationaudit logsretention policiesdata deletiondata lineage

Sensitive data should not automatically be transmitted to external LLM APIs.

The Agent Helper should generally receive:

schemastatisticsrepresentative samplesmetadata

instead of:

entire industrial dataset

unless explicitly required.

This is both:

security+cost+latency

optimization.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 79. Compliance Evidence Generated by Compiler
sections.content:
Every job should produce evidence such as:

input hashinput sourceuser/request IDcompiler versionagent versionrecipe versiontransformation historyvalidation resultswarningserrorsoutput hashtimestampoperator confirmation

This forms the foundation of an audit trail.

sections.heading_text: 90. What the Compiler Guarantees to the Profiler
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 90. What the Compiler Guarantees to the Profiler
sections.content:
The Compiler’s contract with Data Profiler should effectively be:

“I have converted the user’s heterogeneous industrial inputs into a structurally valid, traceable, canonical dataset. You can now concentrate on profiling its statistical and ML-readiness characteristics.”

The Profiler can then start its work.

The complete Stage-1 pipeline is:

INDUSTRIAL USER                               │                               ▼                           JANE                         CHATBOT                               │                               │                    Intent + Data Assets                               │                               ▼                    ┌───────────────────┐                    │ DATA COMPILER     │                    └─────────┬─────────┘                              │                     File Detection                              │                     ZIP Extraction                              │                    Dataset Discovery                              │                              ▼                    ┌───────────────────┐                    │ AGENT HELPER      │                    └─────────┬─────────┘                              │                     Transformation Plan                              │                              ▼                    Plan Validation                              │                              ▼                    Recipe Generation                              │                              ▼                       DAG Execution                              │             ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐             ▼                ▼                ▼           APPEND            JOIN             MERGE             │                │                │             └────────────────┼────────────────┘                              ▼                    Schema Harmonization                              │                    Type Normalization                              │                   Timestamp Normalization                              │                      Unit Normalization                              │                         Validation                              │                        Provenance                              │                              ▼                 AI-CONNEX UNIFIED DATA                              │                    + schema.json                    + metadata.json                    + lineage.json                    + recipe.json                    + quality_report.json                              │                              ▼                    ┌───────────────────┐                    │   DATA PROFILER   │                    └───────────────────┘

The Compiler’s innovation is not:

“We support CSV, Excel and ZIP.”

That alone is not innovative.

The real AI-ConneX innovation is:

The system accepts industrial data in the form in which the industrial user already possesses it, understands relationships between heterogeneous datasets, determines the appropriate transformation strategy with an Agent Helper, validates that strategy deterministically, executes it as a DAG, preserves provenance, and delivers a canonical dataset to downstream AI systems.

That is substantially more powerful.

sections.heading_text: 93. Compiler as an Industrial Data Abstraction Layer
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 93. Compiler as an Industrial Data Abstraction Layer
sections.content:
The Compiler effectively hides:

file formatsschemasencodingjoinsmergestimestampsunitsdata typesdata lineageETL complexity

from the industrial user.

Therefore:

INDUSTRIAL USER                        │                        │              "Here is my data."                        │                        ▼              ┌──────────────────┐              │ AI-ConneX        │              │ DATA COMPILER    │              └────────┬─────────┘                       │                       ▼              "AI-ready data"

This is the fundamental product philosophy of the Data Studio.

Phase R1 — Basic ingestion

CSVXLSXJSONZIP

Phase R2 — Schema intelligence

schema matchingcolumn semanticstimestamp detectionunit detection

Phase R3 — Intelligent composition

appendjoinmergededuplicationtime alignment

Phase R4 — Agent Helper

intent-aware planningschema reasoningtransformation recommendationconfidence scoring

Phase R5 — Industrial hardening

securitysandboxingresource limitsauditprovenancetenant isolation

Phase R6 — Enterprise connectors

SQLS3MESERPSCADAOPC-UAMQTTindustrial historians

Phase R7 — Autonomous Data Engineering

detectunderstandplanvalidateexecutemonitorlearn

The Data Studio Compiler should ultimately implement this principle:

DON'T ASK THE INDUSTRIALIST                         TO FIX THE DATA.                              ↓                   LET AI-ConneX UNDERSTAND IT.                              ↓                      AGENT HELPER                       REASONS ABOUT IT                              ↓                         COMPILER                     VALIDATES + EXECUTES                              ↓                       UNIFIED DATA                              ↓                       DATA PROFILER                              ↓                         ML STUDIO

The Compiler therefore acts as the industrial data translation and compilation boundary of AI-ConneX.

Its responsibility ends when the heterogeneous industrial input has become a validated, canonical, provenance-preserving dataset that Data Profiler can consume without needing to understand the original file-format chaos.

The AI-ConneX Data Studio Compiler Stage-1 is considered complete when the system can take:

one or more arbitrary supported industrial data assets

and automatically:

✓ identify formats✓ safely extract archives✓ inspect datasets✓ discover schemas✓ identify candidate keys✓ identify timestamps✓ identify units✓ detect schema relationships✓ determine append/join/merge requirements✓ use Agent Helper for ambiguous cases✓ validate the proposed plan✓ construct a DAG✓ execute transformations✓ prevent dangerous joins✓ normalize the canonical schema✓ normalize timestamps✓ resolve units where possible✓ detect duplicates✓ preserve source data✓ maintain provenance✓ generate REPORT_1✓ generate unified Parquet✓ generate schema metadata✓ generate lineage metadata✓ provide a clean input contract to Data Profiler

The final handoff is:

COMPILER OUTPUT                         │        ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐        ▼                ▼                ▼   Unified Data       Metadata         Lineage     Parquet             │                │        │                │                │        └────────────────┼────────────────┘                         ▼                 REPORT_1 / QUALITY                         │                         ▼                  DATA PROFILER

That is the formal boundary between Data Studio’s Compiler stage and the Data Profiler stage.

TAS | AI-ConneX — Data Studio Compiler End-of-Stage Verification

sections.heading_text: Chapter 6: Data Studio Compiler POC and Research Documentation
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 6: Data Studio Compiler POC and Research Documentation
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

Data Studio Compiler

Proof of Concept, Research Foundation & Technical Documentation

Agent-Assisted Heterogeneous Industrial Data Integration, Normalization and ValidationStage Report — Compiler / Data Preparation Layer

Figure 6.1: Compiler POC Stage Icon

The AI-ConneX Data Studio Compiler is an agent-assisted industrial data integration and normalization layer. Its purpose is to remove the manual burden of converting heterogeneous industrial datasets into a common structure before analytics, profiling and AI/ML workflows.

Industrial datasets may arrive as CSV, XLSX, JSON, TXT, Parquet, database exports and archives containing multiple files with different schemas. The Compiler discovers the input structure, extracts archives, identifies formats and schemas, determines whether files should be appended, joined, merged or retained separately, performs controlled transformations, normalizes units and timestamps where required, validates the result and produces lineage and a Compilation Report.

Central design principle: the agent recommends; the deterministic Compiler executes and validates. An LLM therefore does not directly modify industrial data.

Industrialists generally care about the engineering problem represented by their data, not about manually converting files or repairing schemas. Conventional preprocessing becomes expensive when datasets contain multiple formats, schema variants, units, timestamp conventions, duplicates, missing values, archives and schema drift.

AI-ConneX introduces a compilation stage between the natural-language Chatbot and the Data Profiler.

Can an agent-assisted compiler automatically ingest heterogeneous industrial datasets and produce a validated unified representation?

Can the system determine when datasets should be appended, joined, merged, transformed or retained separately?

Can semantic/schema inference reduce manual column mapping effort?

Can deterministic validation detect data loss and transformation errors before downstream profiling?

Can transformation lineage make automated industrial data preparation auditable and reproducible?

sections.heading_text: Chapter 7: Data Studio Data Profiler Detailed Documentation
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 7: Data Studio Data Profiler Detailed Documentation
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

Data Studio — Data Profiler

Proof of Concept • R&D • Technical Architecture • Manifest Generation

Industrial Data Intelligence LayerCompiler → Data Profiler → Manifest-UID.jsonStage Report / Compilation Report #1

Figure 7.1: Data Profiler Hero Component Block

The AI-ConneX Data Studio Data Profiler is the intelligence layer immediately after the Data Studio Compiler. The Compiler converts heterogeneous industrial source material into a validated, unified dataset. The Profiler then determines what the compiled dataset actually contains: its structure, semantics, statistical characteristics, quality indicators, relationships, temporal behavior, units, cardinality, distributions and suitability for downstream industrial AI workflows.

The Profiler also reconnects the technical facts discovered from the dataset with the intent established by the AI-ConneX Chatbot and the operational decisions made by the Compiler. These combined facts become a single machine-readable identity document called manifest-UID.json.

The key architectural idea is that a dataset is not considered fully understood merely because it has been normalized. The Compiler answers 'Can we make this data structurally usable?'; the Profiler answers 'What is this data, how does it behave, how reliable is it, and how does it relate to the user's industrial objective?'

sections.content:
{  "intent_id": "ACX-INT-00042",  "industrial_domain": "manufacturing",  "objective": "predict machine failure",  "target_entity": "CNC machine",  "important_signals": ["temperature", "vibration", "motor_speed"],  "time_horizon": "next 24 hours",  "constraints": {    "preserve_source_context": true,    "explainability": "required"  }}

This intent is carried forward rather than discarded. It allows the Profiler to distinguish between generic data statistics and statistics that matter to the industrial objective.

The Profiler can also receive current-stage instructions. For example, an operator may ask it to identify candidate target variables, assess missingness in sensor streams, detect timestamp gaps, or determine whether a dataset is suitable for time-series forecasting.

{  "profiling_request": {    "mode": "industrial_full",    "check_time_series": true,    "check_sensor_quality": true,    "infer_relationships": true,    "generate_manifest": true  }}

The Profiler creates a unified context from three evidence streams:

The resulting manifest is therefore an operational data contract, not merely a profiling report.

Traditional profiling tools generally answer generic questions: number of rows, columns, data types, null counts, unique values, descriptive statistics and distributions. Industrial AI-ConneX requires a broader concept of profiling because industrial datasets are usually temporal, sensor-driven, multi-asset, unit-dependent and purpose-specific.

How can the Profiler automatically characterize heterogeneous industrial variables after normalization?

How can generic statistics be transformed into industrially meaningful metadata?

How can the Profiler distinguish a useful sensor signal from an identifier, categorical label or administrative field?

How can time-series properties such as sampling frequency, gaps, irregular intervals and drift be detected automatically?

How can data quality be quantified without pretending that statistical quality equals engineering correctness?

How can the user's original objective influence which profiling checks receive priority?

How can the resulting metadata become a stable manifest that downstream AI-ConneX modules can consume?

Data profiling has a strong foundation in data quality, schema discovery, metadata management and data integration research. AI-ConneX extends this foundation by making profiling intent-aware and industrial-domain-aware.

Great Expectations provides a useful reference for the separation between expectations, validation and validation results; its current documentation describes validation definitions that associate data batches with expectation suites and return validation results. citeturn0search0turn0search2

Apache DataFusion is relevant to the proposed implementation because it uses Apache Arrow as an in-memory format and provides SQL/DataFrame APIs with support for CSV, Parquet, JSON and Avro, making it a viable high-performance analytical engine for profiling workloads. citeturn0search11turn0search14
Figure 7.2: Compiler Output Entering Data Profiler Pipeline

Dataset row and column counts.

Column names and canonical names.

Physical and logical data types.

Nullable/non-nullable fields.

Candidate identifiers and keys.

Cardinality and uniqueness.

Schema hash and profile version.

For industrial sensor data, generic statistics are insufficient. The Profiler should additionally inspect:

Sampling interval and approximate sampling frequency.

Irregular timestamps.

Missing time windows.

Flat-line sensors.

Constant-value sensors.

Sudden spikes and discontinuities.

Out-of-range observations where engineering limits are known.

Sensor drift and distribution shift.

Noise indicators.

Unit consistency.

Machine/asset/channel cardinality.

Cross-sensor correlation and lag relationships.

Semantic profiling attempts to determine what a field represents, independently of its raw column name. The Profiler can combine canonical names from the Compiler, datatype, units, value ranges, naming patterns, metadata, and domain vocabulary.

Example:Column: temperatureType: floatUnit: °CRange: 21.2–94.7Context: CNC machineCorrelation: bearing_vibrationSemantic classification:asset_signal.temperaturemeasurement_type = temperatureengineering_domain = machine_health

A central AI-ConneX feature is that the Profiler does not treat all columns equally. If the user's objective is predictive maintenance, vibration, temperature, current, pressure and RPM may receive deeper analysis than an administrative operator ID.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 15. How AI-ConneX Overcomes the Failures
sections.content:
Use deterministic computation for all numeric statistics.

Separate observed facts from inferred semantics.

Attach confidence and provenance to inferred metadata.

Preserve source and Compiler lineage.

Use domain-specific profiling policies.

Perform temporal checks for datasets containing timestamps.

Detect candidate identifiers before feature-quality scoring.

Never delete anomalies simply because they are statistically unusual.

Distinguish data-quality warnings from hard failures.

Version every manifest and profile execution.

Make the manifest reproducible from dataset hash + profile configuration + profiler version.

Use an agent only for interpretation and prioritization, not for arithmetic.

Every successful profiling run receives a Profile UID. The UID identifies the profile execution and allows downstream systems to distinguish different versions of the same underlying dataset.

Profile UID example:ACX-PROF-20260814-7F31A2C9Recommended identity inputs:dataset_hashcompiler_job_idprofile_config_hashprofiler_versionexecution_timestamp

The Profile UID should not replace the Dataset UID. Dataset identity, compilation identity and profiling identity should remain separately traceable.

After profiling, AI-ConneX merges the previous Chatbot intent, Compiler metadata and current Profiler findings. The resulting document is named using the manifest UID.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 32. Security, Governance and Compliance Design
sections.content:
Do not expose raw industrial data to an external LLM unless explicitly authorized.

Prefer sending schema summaries, samples or metadata to the agent rather than complete datasets.

Record which metadata was supplied to the agent.

Hash datasets and manifests for integrity.

Keep source artifacts immutable.

Use role-based access control.

Encrypt data in transit and at rest.

Separate tenant/customer namespaces.

Record profiler execution identity and configuration.

Maintain retention policies appropriate to industrial data.
A research-grade evaluation should compare the AI-ConneX Profiler against generic profiling and validation baselines.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 36. Suggested Research Paper Contribution Statement
sections.content: AI-ConneX Data Profiler proposes an intent-aware industrial data profiling layerthat combines deterministic structural/statistical profiling, temporal and sensorquality analysis, semantic inference, provenance from an upstream data compiler,and user-intent context into a unified machine-readable manifest.The approach separates observed dataset facts from inferred semantics and preserveslineage, confidence and reproducibility for downstream industrial AI workflows.

The AI-ConneX Data Profiler converts a compiled dataset from a structurally usable artifact into an understood, contextualized and traceable data asset. Its most important output is therefore not the statistics themselves; it is the machine-readable manifest that preserves why the data exists, how it was compiled, what was discovered about it, how confident those discoveries are, and whether the dataset is suitable for the next AI-ConneX stage.

sections.heading_text: Chapter 8: Data Studio DAG Detailed Documentation
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 8: Data Studio DAG Detailed Documentation
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

Data Studio — DAG Engine

Research • Architecture • Algorithm-Family Discovery • DAG Assignment • POC

Stage 3 Technical DocumentationProfiler → DAG Engine → Downstream AI/ML Execution

Figure 8.1: DAG Engine Component Block

The AI-ConneX Data Studio DAG Engine is the decision and workflow-mapping stage that follows the Data Studio Data Profiler. Its purpose is to inspect the Profile produced for a compiled industrial dataset and determine which algorithm families and executable workflow/DAG templates are technically compatible with that dataset and the user's stated objective.

The DAG Engine does not blindly select an algorithm. It first establishes eligibility, then ranks candidate Family IDs and DAG IDs, records the evidence used for each assignment, rejects incompatible candidates, and produces a machine-readable DAG Plan that downstream training/execution services can consume.

For the supplied AI-ConneX algorithm registry, the current workbook contains 1,993 populated algorithm/DAG entries across 10 algorithm families and 108 algorithm names. Each registry row has a FAMILY_ID, FAMILY_NAME, DAG ID, Algorithm, Variant and optional Special Handling field. The registry is therefore treated as a controlled catalog of candidate workflow templates, not as permission to run every algorithm on every dataset.

sections.heading_text: 2. Stage Position in Overall AI-ConneX Architecture
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 2. Stage Position in Overall AI-ConneX Architecture
sections.content: USER | vCHATBOT |  intent_uid / objective / constraints vDATA STUDIO COMPILER |  unified dataset + schema + lineage vDATA STUDIO DATA PROFILER |  profile_uid + dataset facts + quality + semantics vDATA STUDIO DAG ENGINE  <---- Algorithm Family/DAG Registry | +--> Eligibility analysis +--> Family identification +--> Candidate DAG discovery +--> Constraint filtering +--> Ranking +--> Explainability / evidence +--> DAG instantiation +--> Compliance Report #3 | vDAG PLAN / DAG MANIFEST | vMODEL TRAINING / SIMULATION / OPTIMIZATION / EXECUTION STAGES

Industrial datasets do not arrive with an explicit statement such as 'use XGBoost classification with these features'. The dataset may instead contain sensor measurements, production records, maintenance events, images, text, temporal sequences, control signals or multiple entities. The DAG stage must infer which classes of computational workflows are possible without confusing statistical compatibility with business suitability.

The R&D problem is therefore a constrained recommendation and workflow-construction problem:

Given:  Manifest-UID  + Dataset Profile  + User Intent  + Algorithm/DAG RegistryDetermine:  1. Which problem families are plausible?  2. Which registered DAG IDs are eligible?  3. Which candidates violate constraints?  4. Which candidates are strongest and why?  5. How can the selected candidate be instantiated reproducibly?

Automatically map profile characteristics to one or more algorithm families.

Discover every registry DAG that satisfies hard compatibility constraints.

Rank candidates using intent relevance, data characteristics and operational constraints.

Keep multiple families when the dataset legitimately supports multiple problem formulations.

Prevent an LLM from inventing algorithms or DAG IDs not present in the registry.

Expose evidence and reasons behind every family/DAG assignment.

Produce deterministic results for deterministic inputs and configuration.

Generate a downstream-ready executable DAG specification.

sections.heading_text: 6. Source Registry Analysis — Supplied Algorithm Workbook
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 6. Source Registry Analysis — Supplied Algorithm Workbook
sections.content:
The supplied algorithm_families_complete.xlsx was inspected as the registry source for this stage. It contains 1,993 populated rows, 10 Family IDs, 108 distinct algorithm names and 1,993 distinct DAG IDs in the populated registry rows. 1,906 rows contain a Special Handling value.

The workbook is therefore a concrete part of the POC design. The DAG Engine should load this registry through a versioned registry adapter rather than hard-code the 1,993 mappings into application logic.

{  "intent_uid": "ACX-INT-00042",  "domain": "manufacturing",  "objective": "predict_machine_failure",  "task": "predictive_maintenance",  "target": "failure_event",  "constraints": {    "explainability": "required",    "latency": "low"  }}
{  "dataset_uid": "ACX-IND-00042",  "artifact": "dataset.parquet",  "schema": "schema.json",  "lineage": "lineage.json",  "compilation_report": "report_1.json"}

{  "profile_uid": "ACX-PROF-....",  "manifest_uid": "ACX-MAN-00042",  "task_hints": ["classification", "time_series"],  "candidate_target": "failure_event",  "time_index": "timestamp",  "features": ["temperature", "vibration", "motor_speed"],  "quality": {...},  "temporal": {...},  "semantic": {...}}

The DAG Engine's primary input should be the manifest-UID.json from the Profiler stage. The Chatbot intent remains traceable inside that manifest and is not discarded.

Family selection should be multi-label rather than forced single-label whenever the evidence supports multiple problem formulations. For example, a manufacturing dataset with a failure label and dense timestamped sensor streams may support both F1 CLASSIFICATION and F5 TIME-SERIES. The DAG Engine should represent the distinction between 'problem family' and 'execution strategy'.

Example:Primary family: F1 CLASSIFICATIONSecondary family: F5 TIME-SERIESReason:  target = failure_event  temporal structure = strong  sequence-aware candidate workflows = eligible

Figure 8.2: Data Profiler Inputs Feeding DAG Engine
A DAG becomes eligible only when all hard constraints are satisfied. Soft characteristics affect ranking rather than automatic rejection.

A proposed score separates feasibility from preference. A candidate that fails a hard requirement receives zero eligibility regardless of its soft score.

Eligibility(DAG) =  all(hard_constraints == PASS)Score(DAG) =  0.30 * intent_relevance+ 0.20 * data_compatibility+ 0.15 * target_compatibility+ 0.10 * temporal_compatibility+ 0.10 * scale_compatibility+ 0.05 * quality_robustness+ 0.05 * explainability_fit+ 0.05 * operational_fit

The weights are configuration, not scientific constants. The final research paper should report the exact weights and an ablation study.

Profile:  target = failure_event  target_type = binary  timestamp = present  sensor_features = temperature, vibration, rpm  rows = 999842  modality = tabular + temporal  objective = predictive maintenanceFamily candidates:  F1 CLASSIFICATION       -> ELIGIBLE  F5 TIME-SERIES          -> ELIGIBLE  F3 ANOMALY DETECTION    -> CONDITIONAL  F2 REGRESSION           -> REJECT  F10 COMPUTER VISION     -> REJECTDAG selection:  rank eligible registry DAG IDs using compatibility + intent + constraints.

sections.heading_text: 13. Special Handling Is a First-Class Input
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 13. Special Handling Is a First-Class Input
sections.content: The supplied workbook contains Special Handling information for 1,906 of 1,993 populated entries. The DAG Engine must not treat this field as documentation-only. It should be converted into machine-readable execution requirements wherever possible.

A registry DAG ID identifies a template. The actual dataset workflow is created only after binding runtime context.

DAG_XXX (registry template)        |        +-- dataset_uid        +-- manifest_uid        +-- feature set        +-- target        +-- train/validation/test policy        +-- preprocessing requirements        +-- algorithm parameters        +-- resource policy        |        vACX-RUN-DAG-XXXX (instantiated DAG)

This separation prevents the registry from becoming polluted with dataset-specific executions.

DAG:  INPUT    |    v  schema_validation    |    v  time_split    |    +--> feature_cleaning    |    +--> imbalance_check    |    v  algorithm_node    |    v  validation    |    v  evaluation    |    v  model_artifact

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 17. How AI-ConneX Overcomes These Failures
sections.content:
Registry-first architecture: the system may only recommend DAG IDs that exist in the approved registry.

Two-stage filtering: hard feasibility first, soft ranking second.

Profile-driven discovery: data modality, target, cardinality, temporal behavior and quality directly constrain candidates.

Intent-aware ranking: the user's actual industrial objective affects candidate preference.

Special Handling compiler: registry text is normalized into execution requirements.

Evidence graph: every recommendation points back to profile facts, intent fields or registry properties.

Top-K output: downstream experimentation can compare multiple viable candidates.

Versioned registry snapshots: every run is reproducible against the exact registry used.

Static DAG validation: schema, cycles, missing dependencies, unsupported nodes and resource rules are checked before execution.

Agent containment: the agent may interpret and rank evidence but cannot invent or directly execute arbitrary DAGs.

DAG AGENT HELPER                        |                        v                Registry Retrieval                        |                        v                Candidate Analysis                        |                        v             Structured Recommendation                        |                        v             DETERMINISTIC VALIDATOR              /                    \           PASS                    FAIL            |                       |            v                       v      DAG Instantiation        Rejection Reason            |            v        DAG Validator            |            v        DAG Plan

{  "family_id": "F1",  "dag_id": "DAG_XXX",  "decision": "ELIGIBLE",  "confidence": 0.94,  "evidence": [    "target_type=binary",    "target=failure_event",    "intent=predictive_maintenance"  ],  "registry_version": "2026.08",  "requires": ["class_balance_check"]}

The agent cannot create a new DAG ID. If no registry candidate is suitable, it must return NO_COMPATIBLE_DAG rather than fabricate one.
These are proposed baselines and should be pinned in a lockfile after the project's POC compatibility test. The DAG Engine itself should not depend on an LLM for deterministic graph operations.

sections.heading_text: 28. What This Stage Does with Chatbot Output
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 28. What This Stage Does with Chatbot Output
sections.content:
The DAG Engine does not replace the Chatbot's intent. It uses that intent as a decision constraint. For example, 'predict machine failure' supplies a classification/predictive-maintenance objective, but the Profiler determines whether the dataset actually contains a suitable target and temporal structure.

CHATBOT SAYS:  objective = predict machine failurePROFILER OBSERVES:  failure_event exists  binary target  timestamp exists  sensor streams existDAG ENGINE CONCLUDES:  F1 classification -> eligible  F5 time-series -> eligible  F2 regression -> not suitable for this target

Because the DAG stage is downstream of the Data Profiler, its normal output is not another Data Profiler input. The canonical next-stage input is a DAG Plan / instantiated DAG specification. If the phrase 'input for the Data Profiler' is retained in the overall documentation, it should refer to the Profiler's upstream input contract, not this stage's output.

Recommended canonical downstream contract: dag_plan.json.

The supplied workbook provides the registry needed for a meaningful POC. The POC should combine it with synthetic/realistic industrial manifests generated by the previous stages.

POC INPUTS  manifest-ACX-MAN-00042.json  algorithm_families_complete.xlsx              |              v        REGISTRY IMPORT              |              v      FAMILY DISCOVERY              |              v      HARD FILTERING              |              v       DAG CANDIDATES              |              v       SCORE + RANK              |              v      DAG VALIDATION              |              v         DAG PLAN              |              +--> report_3.json              +--> evidence.json

All registry rows are imported without losing FAMILY_ID or DAG ID.

Duplicate DAG IDs are rejected by registry validation.

Every candidate DAG returned by the engine exists in the registry.

No candidate is selected when a mandatory target/modality requirement is absent.

At least one realistic industrial benchmark produces sensible family assignments.

Hard rejection reasons are recorded.

Top-K ranking is deterministic under identical registry, manifest and configuration.

Generated DAGs pass cycle and dependency validation.

Report #3 is generated for every completed discovery run.

Registry version and hash are preserved in the output.

H1: Profile-aware filtering reduces the candidate search space without materially reducing relevant DAG recall.

H2: Intent-aware ranking improves Top-K candidate relevance compared with profile-only ranking.

H3: Registry-constrained agent assistance reduces invalid/hallucinated algorithm selections compared with unconstrained LLM recommendation.

H4: Explicit Special Handling constraints reduce execution-time incompatibilities.

H5: Evidence-backed DAG assignment improves human auditability compared with opaque recommendation.

AI-ConneX should not claim that DAG orchestration, AutoML, algorithm recommendation or graph validation are individually novel. The defensible contribution is the integration of these capabilities into an industrial data pipeline where the Profiler's observed dataset characteristics and the Chatbot's intent are joined with a versioned algorithm/DAG registry, producing auditable, constrained and reproducible candidate DAGs.

Proposed contribution:Intent  +Observed Data Profile  +Versioned Algorithm Registry  +Constraint Engine  +Evidence-backed Ranking  =Industrial DAG Discovery and Instantiation Layer

Never permit arbitrary code generation as a substitute for registered DAG nodes.

Registry entries must be authenticated/versioned and preferably immutable after release.

Agent tool calls must be allow-listed.

Dataset and manifest access must be authorization-controlled.

DAG plans must carry source manifest hash and registry version.

Resource limits must be validated before execution.

Every selected DAG must have an audit trail.

Rejected candidates should be retained for explainability/debugging.

Rahm, E., & Bernstein, P. A. (2001). A survey of approaches to automatic schema matching. The VLDB Journal, 10, 334–350.

Doan, A., Halevy, A. Y., & Ives, Z. G. Principles of Data Integration. Morgan Kaufmann.

Feurer, M., & Hutter, F. (2019). Hyperparameter Optimization. In Automated Machine Learning: Methods, Systems, Challenges.

Thornton, C., Hutter, F., Hoos, H. H., & Leyton-Brown, K. (2013). Auto-WEKA: Combined Selection and Hyperparameter Optimization of Classification Algorithms. KDD.

Leite, J. C. S. do P., & Doorn, J. H. (2000). Data flow and process-oriented approaches to workflow/DAG reasoning.

NetworkX documentation — directed graphs, DAG utilities and topological algorithms.

Apache Arrow documentation — columnar interchange and analytical data representation.

The Data Studio DAG Engine converts 'what the dataset is' and 'what the user wants' into 'what computational workflows are legitimately possible'. The Profiler provides evidence; the registry provides the permitted algorithm vocabulary; the DAG Engine applies constraints and ranking; and the downstream execution layer receives a validated DAG Plan.

The most important control is that the system must never equate an algorithm being mathematically applicable with an algorithm being operationally appropriate. AI-ConneX therefore separates eligibility, ranking, instantiation and execution.

sections.heading_text: Chapter 9: Data Studio Recipe Orchestrator Detailed Documentation
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 9: Data Studio Recipe Orchestrator Detailed Documentation
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

Data Studio — Recipe Orchestrator

PREPARE → FE → STEM → Metrics → Manifest Binding

Stage 4 Technical / R&D Documentation

Figure 9.1: Recipe Orchestrator Stage Icon

The AI-ConneX Data Studio Recipe Orchestrator is the execution-planning stage that follows DAG discovery. It pulls approved recipes for three principal execution domains: PREPARE (cleaning and dataset preparation), FE (feature engineering), and STEM (split, train and evaluate metrics). It then composes these recipes into an executable, dependency-aware workflow and binds the complete recipe lineage back to the manifest-UID.

The word 'recipe' is deliberately used as a controlled, parameterized implementation template rather than as arbitrary generated code. A recipe describes what operation is performed, which inputs it consumes, what parameters it requires, what artifact it emits, what validation it performs and how it is linked to the manifest.

The architecture is designed to prevent the common failure where preprocessing is performed outside the training pipeline and therefore leaks information from validation/test data. scikit-learn's Pipeline documentation explicitly describes chained transformers and estimators and notes that pipeline composition helps avoid leakage by fitting transformations on training data within the pipeline. citeturn0search0turn0search9

CHATBOT  |  vCOMPILER  |  vDATA PROFILER  |  vDAG ENGINE  |  | Family IDs + DAG IDs + selected DAG  vRECIPE ORCHESTRATOR  |  +--> PREPARE recipes  +--> FE recipes  +--> STEM recipes  +--> Manifest binding  +--> Recipe validation  +--> Dependency graph  +--> Run specification  |  vEXECUTION ENGINE  |  +--> prepared dataset  +--> feature dataset  +--> trained model  +--> metrics  +--> run lineage / artifacts

This stage should be treated as an execution-plan compiler. It does not independently decide the business objective; that comes from the Chatbot and Manifest. It does not independently invent a model; the selected algorithm/DAG comes from the previous DAG stage.

A recipe is a versioned, typed, executable template. It is analogous to a function or workflow component with an explicit contract.

Recipe =  recipe_id  recipe_version  stage  inputs  parameters  preconditions  operation  outputs  metrics / validation  resource_requirements  lineage  security_policy

sections.heading_text: 4. Why the Recipe Orchestrator Is Needed
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 4. Why the Recipe Orchestrator Is Needed
sections.content:
Industrial datasets require different cleaning and preparation policies depending on the Profile and selected DAG.

Feature engineering must be reproducible and must not leak information from held-out data.

Training and evaluation need a single controlled execution contract.

Model metrics need to remain linked to the exact feature and dataset versions used.

An industrial user should not have to manually connect preprocessing, features, training and evaluation.

Recipe selection must be deterministic and registry-grounded.

Every transformation must be auditable from output back to manifest-UID.

The research problem is to transform a selected DAG and dataset manifest into a safe, parameterized and reproducible execution graph. The system must decide which PREPARE and FE recipes are compatible, bind them to the STEM recipe implied by the selected DAG, and preserve lineage across every artifact.

Input:  manifest-UID  profile  intent  selected Family/DAG  recipe registryOutput:  executable recipe graph  + recipe parameters  + artifact contracts  + lineage  + validation policy  + run manifest

Build a controlled recipe registry.

Map profile facts to recipe eligibility.

Select PREPARE recipes without destroying information unnecessarily.

Select FE recipes compatible with the selected DAG and data type.

Construct leakage-safe split/train/evaluation execution.

Bind every recipe and artifact to the manifest-UID.

Provide deterministic and auditable recipe selection.

Permit parallel execution only where dependency rules allow it.

Prevent arbitrary agent-generated transformations from entering production execution.

sections.heading_text: 8. How the Orchestrator Uses Chatbot Intent
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 8. How the Orchestrator Uses Chatbot Intent
sections.content:
The Chatbot's intent is not used as a generic prompt to generate code. It becomes a constraint on recipe selection. For example, if the user requests predictive maintenance with low latency and explainability, the orchestrator can prefer compact feature sets, deterministic preprocessing and an evaluation set appropriate to the operational requirement.

CHATBOT:  "predict machine failure"MANIFEST:  binary target  sensor streams  timestamp  missing values  categorical machine_idDAG:  classification + time-seriesRECIPE ORCHESTRATOR:  PREPARE -> timestamp validation + missing-value policy  FE      -> lag/rolling features + encoding  STEM    -> temporal split + classifier + classification metrics

Recipes should be stored separately from algorithm/DAG registry entries. The DAG registry answers 'which computational workflow/model family is appropriate?'. The Recipe Registry answers 'how should the selected workflow's data preparation, feature construction and training/evaluation steps be executed?'.

Manifest + DAG Plan       |       vRecipe Eligibility Engine       |       +------------------+       |                  |       v                  vPREPARE registry       FE registry       |                  |       +--------+---------+                |                v        STEM recipe registry                |                v       Recipe dependency graph                |                v       Manifest binding layer                |                v        Validated Run Plan
PREPARE is responsible for transforming compiled data into a clean, consistent, model-consumable dataset while preserving lineage and avoiding irreversible changes unless explicitly permitted.
Feature Engineering transforms prepared data into model-specific features. Feature recipes must declare whether they are fit-time, transform-time or deterministic/stateless.

Any feature transformation that learns statistics from data must be fitted only on the training partition and then applied to validation/test data. Pipeline-based execution is preferred because it encapsulates transformation and estimator steps and can avoid leakage when fit is performed on training data. citeturn0search0turn0search9

CORRECTRAW | vSPLIT |------------------| v                  vTRAIN              TEST | vFIT FE | +--> transform TRAIN | +--> transform TEST using TRAIN-fitted FE | vTRAIN MODEL | vEVALUATE TEST

For time-series data, the split must additionally respect temporal ordering; a random split may expose future information.

STEM is the model execution spine: Split → Train → Evaluate Metrics. The selected DAG supplies the model/algorithm identity, while the recipe registry supplies the operational steps.

PREPARE   |   vFE   |   vSPLIT   |   +--> TRAIN   |   +--> VALIDATION   |   vMODEL FIT   |   vPREDICT   |   vMETRICS   |   vMODEL + METRICS + LINEAGE

The split recipe must be selected from Profile temporal/entity characteristics rather than always applying a generic random train_test_split.

Figure 9.3: STEM Execution Spine — Split Policy Handoff to Model Training

The STEM training node consumes the selected algorithm from the DAG Plan and the feature artifact from FE. It must record implementation version, hyperparameters, random seed, hardware/runtime and input hashes.

TRAIN INPUT  feature_artifact_hash  target_column  algorithm_id  algorithm_version  hyperparameters  random_seed  resource_policyTRAIN OUTPUT  model_artifact  training_log  training_metadata

Metrics are selected based on the task and user intent rather than using one universal metric.

Metric thresholds should be expressed in the manifest/run policy when the industrial user has explicit acceptance requirements.

Figure 9.4: STEM Execution Spine — Model Training to Evaluation Metrics

Manifest binding is the central responsibility of this stage. Each recipe execution must carry the manifest UID, profile UID, intent UID, DAG ID and registry versions.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 21. How AI-ConneX Overcomes the Failures
sections.content:
Recipe Registry: execution uses approved, versioned recipes rather than unconstrained code.

Capability contracts: each recipe declares required input types, task type, estimator capabilities and resource needs.

Manifest binding: every artifact carries immutable upstream identifiers.

Leakage guard: learned preprocessing is fitted inside the correct training scope.

Temporal guard: timestamped datasets use chronology-aware split policies.

Feature audit: generated features record source columns and transformations.

Metric policy: evaluation metrics are determined before execution and cannot be silently replaced.

Checkpointing: every recipe emits a validated artifact and metadata.

Idempotency: recipe runs use deterministic run IDs and input hashes.

Agent containment: agents may recommend or parameterize recipes but cannot bypass registry validation.

RECIPE AGENT                      |        +-------------+-------------+        |             |             |        v             v             v     PREPARE         FE           STEM     Registry      Registry      Registry        |             |             |        +-------------+-------------+                      |                      v              Capability Validator                      |                      v               Recipe Composer                      |                      v               DAG/Graph Validator                      |                      v                Run Plan

The agent is an assistant to the deterministic orchestration layer, not the authority. The final recipe IDs, versions, dependencies and parameters must pass schema and policy validation.

{  "recipe_id": "FE-ROLLING-004",  "version": "2.0.1",  "stage": "FE",  "inputs": ["prepared_dataset"],  "requires": {    "timestamp": true,    "numeric_columns": true  },  "parameters": {    "windows": [5, 15, 60]  },  "outputs": ["feature_dataset"],  "leakage_policy": "fit_on_train_only",  "resource_class": "medium"}

PREPARE must complete before dependent FE operations.

Stateless FE operations may execute before/after split only when their semantics guarantee no leakage; default policy is to keep them inside the pipeline.

Learned FE operations must be fit only on training data.

SPLIT must precede model training.

TRAIN must precede predictions and model-dependent metrics.

EVALUATE may consume held-out predictions and labels.

Independent diagnostic computations may run in parallel after their dependencies are satisfied.

Every node must declare its artifact schema.

The exact versions should be frozen in `pyproject.toml`/lockfile after POC compatibility testing. scikit-learn's current pipeline model supports chained transformers and estimators and explicitly documents leakage-avoidance benefits of pipeline composition. citeturn0search5turn0search9

The DAG stage chooses the computational direction; the Recipe Orchestrator translates that direction into controlled PREPARE, FE and STEM operations; the manifest binds the complete chain into one auditable execution identity.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Appendix C — Important Clarification on Stage Naming
sections.content:
The requested description calls this 'Data Studio's DAG', but architecturally it is better represented as a sub-stage after DAG discovery: **DAG Execution / Recipe Orchestrator**. The previous DAG Engine discovers and selects Family/DAG IDs; this Recipe Orchestrator pulls PREPARE/FE/STEM recipes and materializes the selected DAG into an executable run plan. Keeping those responsibilities separate prevents DAG discovery from becoming coupled to implementation details.

sections.heading_text: Chapter 10: Data Studio PREPARE Node Detailed Documentation
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 10: Data Studio PREPARE Node Detailed Documentation
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

DATA STUDIO — PREPARE NODE

Industrial Data Preparation, Validation & Readiness Layer — Technical Documentation

Compliance Report #5

Figure 10.1: PREPARE Node Hero Component Block

The PREPARE Node is the first execution node after the AI-ConneX Data Studio Brain. The Brain decides what should happen; PREPARE makes the selected dataset physically and logically ready for downstream Feature Engineering (FE), Split, Training and Evaluation (STEM).

The PREPARE Node receives the canonical dataset, manifest-UID.json, DAG assignment, recipe plan, lineage and user-intent context produced by earlier stages. It does not rediscover the entire problem from scratch. Instead, it executes controlled preparation operations authorized by the manifest, selected DAG and PREPARE recipe.

CHATBOT  intent     |     vBRAIN  Compiler -> Profiler -> DAG Assigner -> Recipe Orchestrator     |     +-------------------------------+     |                               |     v                               vcanonical dataset              manifest-UID.json     |                               |     +---------------+---------------+                     |                     v              PREPARE NODE                     |          +----------+----------+          |          |          |       Validate    Clean      Standardize          |          |          |          +----------+----------+                     |                     v             PREPARED DATASET                     |                     v                FE / STEM

PREPARE is responsible for data readiness, not model intelligence. Its job is to make the dataset structurally valid, semantically consistent, quality-controlled and safe for the selected downstream workflow.

Figure 10.2: Intent & Recipe Flow — The Brain to PREPARE Node

Validate that the input matches the manifest and expected schema.

Apply approved cleaning and normalization operations.

Resolve or quarantine missing, malformed and invalid records according to policy.

Normalize timestamps, units, categories and identifiers where required.

Handle duplicates according to explicit rules.

Apply domain-aware filtering only when justified.

Preserve lineage for every transformation.

Produce a prepared dataset and a preparation/compliance report.

Block unsafe transformations instead of silently changing industrial data.

Emit metadata needed by FE and STEM.

prepare_input/  dataset/    canonical.parquet  manifest/    manifest-UID.json  brain/    dag_plan.json    recipe_plan.json  intent/    intent.json  lineage/    lineage.json  policies/    preparation_policy.yaml

The manifest is the principal control document. It describes what the Brain believes the data is; PREPARE verifies that reality has not changed between profiling/planning and execution.

sections.heading_text: 5. What PREPARE Receives from the Previous Chatbot Stage
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 5. What PREPARE Receives from the Previous Chatbot Stage
sections.content:
The Chatbot's output is not directly converted into cleaning instructions. It is carried through the Brain as user intent. This distinction is critical: a user might say 'remove bad sensor readings', but the exact meaning of 'bad' must be resolved using the profile, industrial constraints and registered recipes.

CHATBOT OUTPUT{  "intent_uid": "ACX-INT-00042",  "objective": "predict machine failure",  "target": "failure_event",  "constraints": {      "near_real_time": false,      "explainability": "required"  },  "domain_context": "...",  "user_constraints": [...]}          |          vBRAIN / MANIFEST          |          vPREPARE  uses intent as CONTEXT + CONSTRAINT,  not as unrestricted executable instructions.

The R&D challenge is not 'how to clean a dataframe'. The real challenge is deciding what may safely be changed in industrial data without destroying operational meaning.

Industrial sensor data can contain missing measurements, transient spikes, maintenance windows, duplicated events, clock drift, unit inconsistencies, impossible physical values and categorical codes that changed between systems. A generic cleaning script can easily convert legitimate events into apparently clean but incorrect data.

Therefore AI-ConneX PREPARE is policy-driven, manifest-aware and lineage-preserving.

sections.heading_text: 10. PREPARE Design Principle: Never Clean Blindly
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 10. PREPARE Design Principle: Never Clean Blindly
sections.content:
The central principle is: every material transformation must be explainable by a rule, recipe, policy or explicit user/domain constraint.

TRANSFORMATION      |      +--> Why is this column affected?      +--> Why this operation?      +--> Which recipe?      +--> Which policy?      +--> Which manifest evidence?      +--> How many records changed?      +--> Can original values be recovered?      |      vLINEAGE EVENT

Before modifying values, PREPARE verifies that the dataset still resembles the dataset that was profiled.

Column presence.

Column names and aliases.

Data types.

Nullable status.

Expected key fields.

Target availability.

Timestamp availability.

Schema fingerprint.

Expected row/partition structure.

Schema mismatch should normally stop or quarantine the run rather than automatically 'fixing' a major drift. Minor compatible drift may be handled by registered compatibility rules.

Missingness is treated as information first and a defect second. The strategy depends on column role, temporal structure, entity structure and recipe requirements.

The chosen operation is recorded with counts before and after transformation.

Duplicates are not necessarily errors. PREPARE distinguishes exact duplicates, key duplicates and legitimate repeated measurements.

Exact duplicate rows.

Duplicate business keys.

Repeated sensor measurements at the same timestamp.

Duplicate records caused by source replay.

Multiple valid events sharing the same timestamp.

The policy should specify whether to retain first/last, aggregate, reconcile, quarantine or reject.

PREPARE can enforce physical or business-domain constraints when they are available. Examples include negative runtime hours, impossible temperatures, invalid status codes, impossible timestamps and values outside instrument limits.

Hard constraints should be deterministic. Soft statistical anomalies should not automatically be treated as errors.

An outlier detector is not automatically an outlier remover. A machine failure, pressure spike or emergency shutdown can be the most valuable observation in a predictive-maintenance dataset.

Flag rather than delete by default.

Use domain thresholds when available.

Use statistical thresholds only as supporting evidence.

Consider maintenance/event context.

Keep an original-value lineage.

Allow downstream DAG/recipe to decide whether flagged points are excluded.

Parse supported timestamp formats.

Normalize timezone handling.

Check monotonicity where required.

Detect impossible/future timestamps.

Detect duplicate timestamps within entity.

Compute sampling interval statistics.

Flag gaps and bursts.

Preserve original timestamp when conversion is material.

Temporal correctness is especially important because a technically clean dataset can still be invalid if preparation uses information from the future.

Industrial datasets frequently mix engineering units. PREPARE should maintain a unit registry and record conversions rather than merely renaming columns.

temperature:  source_unit: F  target_unit: C  conversion: (F - 32) * 5/9pressure:  source_unit: psi  target_unit: kPa  conversion: psi * 6.894757

Every conversion should record source unit, target unit, conversion rule and recipe version.

Normalize whitespace/casing only where semantically safe.

Map known aliases using a controlled dictionary.

Do not collapse identifiers that differ only because they appear similar.

Preserve original category values for lineage.

Validate category domains when a controlled vocabulary exists.

AI-ConneX can implement declarative validation using a framework such as Great Expectations or an internal equivalent. Great Expectations describes Expectations as verifiable assertions about data and provides reusable validation/checkpoint concepts and validation results. citeturn0search8turn0search6

Expectation Suite      |      vCheckpoint / Validation Run      |      +--> PASS      |      +--> WARN      |      +--> FAIL      |      vValidation Report

For an industrial deployment, the project should define which expectations are hard gates and which are warnings. A validation framework is an implementation choice; the AI-ConneX contract is the important architectural concept.

A columnar representation such as Apache Arrow/Parquet is recommended for the prepared artifact because Arrow defines a language-independent in-memory format and IPC/data transport model, while Parquet provides practical persistent columnar storage. Arrow is explicitly designed for efficient data interchange and in-memory analytics. citeturn0search0turn0search4

RAW / COMPILED       |       vArrow-compatible execution       |       vParquet / Arrow prepared artifact       |       +--> FE       +--> STEM

recipe:  id: PREPARE-TEMPORAL-001  version: 1.2.0  inputs:    required:      - timestamp      - entity_id  operations:    - validate_schema    - parse_timestamp    - normalize_timezone    - validate_missingness    - quarantine_invalid_timestamps    - validate_sampling_gaps  outputs:    dataset    validation_report    lineage  safety:    destructive_operations: false    leakage_guard: enabled

Instead of deleting uncertain records, PREPARE should preferentially move them to a quarantine artifact with a reason code.

prepared/  data.parquetquarantine/  records.parquet  reasons.jsonreasons:  INVALID_TIMESTAMP  UNKNOWN_UNIT  SCHEMA_MISMATCH  DOMAIN_VIOLATION  DUPLICATE_CONFLICT  TYPE_CONVERSION_FAILURE

This is especially important for industry because an anomalous record may be the evidence of the exact failure the model is intended to detect.

Every PREPARE run should provide accounting:

input_rowsoutput_rowsquarantined_rowsdropped_rowsmodified_rowscolumns_modifiednulls_beforenulls_afterduplicates_beforeduplicates_aftervalidation_passedvalidation_failed

A run without this accounting should not be considered fully auditable.

manifest_uid    |    +--> prepare_run_uid            |            +--> input_hash            +--> recipe_id/version            +--> policy_id/version            +--> operation_001            +--> operation_002            +--> ...            +--> output_hash            +--> quarantine_hash

sections.heading_text: 27. What PREPARE Outputs to Feature Engineering
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 27. What PREPARE Outputs to Feature Engineering
sections.content:
PREPARE must not simply output a dataframe. It outputs a controlled dataset package.

FE INPUT PACKAGE  |  +-- prepared_dataset.parquet  +-- prepared_manifest.json  +-- schema_fingerprint.json  +-- validation_results.json  +-- lineage.json  +-- recipe_reference.json  +-- target_definition.json  +-- temporal_policy.json  +-- entity_policy.json

Figure 10.3: Handoff — PREPARE Clean Package to Feature Engineering

FE can therefore determine which columns are safe and available, what target is expected, how time/entity boundaries should be respected and what transformations have already occurred.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 28. Relationship to the Data Profiler
sections.content:
The user requested how PREPARE outputs back into the Data Profiler. Architecturally, PREPARE should not replace the Brain's original manifest. Instead, it should emit a post-preparation validation/profile artifact that can be consumed by a downstream validation profiler or used to update the manifest lineage.

ORIGINAL PROFILER       |       vmanifest-UID.json       |       vPREPARE       |       +--> prepared_dataset       +--> prepare_report_5       +--> post_prepare_profile.json       |       vFE / STEMOPTIONAL FEEDBACK:post_prepare_profile       |       vData Quality / Profiler monitoring

This distinction prevents circular architecture: the original Profiler describes the input to planning, while a post-prepare validation profile verifies the result of preparation.

Rows removed/quarantined.

New missingness statistics.

Schema after preparation.

Distribution changes.

Category cardinality changes.

Timestamp gap statistics.

Unit-normalization evidence.

Validation results.

Potential new anomalies introduced by transformation.

Preparation must distinguish operations that can be performed globally from operations that learn parameters from data. Any operation whose parameters are learned from observations—such as imputation statistics, scaling statistics or category dictionaries—must be scoped correctly when the downstream workflow requires train/test separation.

A strong design is to allow PREPARE to perform structural, deterministic validation globally, while learned transformations are represented as recipe components whose fitting scope is controlled by the downstream STEM split. This is an architectural safeguard rather than a blanket rule that all cleaning must happen after splitting.
Example: converting psi to kPa is PREPARE. Creating a 30-minute rolling pressure mean is FE. The boundary must remain explicit for lineage and leakage control.

PREPARE should not train models. STEM owns split, training and evaluation. If a preparation decision depends on the split—for example, fitting an imputer or scaler—its fitting operation should be represented so STEM can execute it within the correct training scope.

One major architectural failure would be allowing an agent to decide that every problem can be solved by a generic cleaning template. AI-ConneX avoids this by requiring the Recipe Orchestrator to select registered PREPARE recipes based on the manifest and DAG constraints.

Agent suggestion      |      vRecipe Registry      |      vCapability / Schema Validator      |      +--> valid --> execute      |      +--> invalid --> stop / ask

Traditional ETL pipelines sometimes overwrite or discard source values. AI-ConneX uses immutable raw/compiled artifacts, output versioning and quarantine so that a preparation mistake does not destroy the evidence.

Raw data immutable.

Compiled data immutable.

Prepared output versioned.

Quarantine retained.

Hashes recorded.

Transformations recorded.

The most dangerous PREPARE failure is a dataset that passes basic validation but has lost business meaning. Examples include deleting failure spikes, collapsing machine IDs, converting timezones incorrectly or imputing long sensor outages.

AI-ConneX therefore separates structural validity from semantic validity and requires domain-aware rules where available.

Use columnar storage.

Process only required columns.

Partition large datasets.

Stream/chunk expensive transformations.

Push filtering/aggregation to a query engine when appropriate.

Use lazy execution where supported.

Record resource usage in the run report.

Exact versions should be frozen in a lockfile after POC compatibility testing. Apache Arrow is particularly appropriate as an interoperability layer because it is language-independent and designed for data interchange/in-memory analytics. citeturn0search0turn0search4

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 54. Research Contribution of AI-ConneX PREPARE
sections.content:
The proposed contribution is not another generic data-cleaning library. AI-ConneX PREPARE is a manifest- and recipe-controlled industrial preparation node positioned after a reasoning Brain. Its distinctive architectural hypothesis is that preparation should be generated from the combination of user intent, observed data profile, selected DAG and registered recipe, while every material transformation remains auditable.

This should be experimentally validated against conventional scripts, generic ETL pipelines and baseline automated preprocessing systems before claiming superiority.

Least-privilege access to source and output datasets.

Encryption in transit and at rest.

No credentials in recipes or manifests.

PII/sensitive-field classification before transformations.

Immutable raw artifacts.

Role-based approval for destructive operations.

Audit logs for exceptions.

Versioned policies and recipes.

Artifact hashes for integrity.

sections.heading_text: 58. PREPARE as an Industrial Control Point
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 58. PREPARE as an Industrial Control Point
sections.content:
The PREPARE Node should be treated as a controlled checkpoint rather than a simple preprocessing script. Once PREPARE passes, downstream FE/STEM can rely on a stronger contract. If it fails, the pipeline stops before feature engineering or training consumes corrupted or ambiguous data.

RAW/COMPILED     |     v   PREPARE     |   [CONTROL]  /         FAIL        PASS |           |STOP         v          FEATURE ENGINEERING               |               v              STEM

AI-CONNEX DATA STUDIO                    BRAIN  +-----------------------------------------------+  | Chatbot Intent                                |  |      ↓                                        |  | Compiler → Profiler → DAG Assigner            |  |                         ↓                      |  |                 Recipe Orchestrator           |  +-------------------------+---------------------+                            |                 manifest + dataset +                 DAG + recipe + lineage                            |                            v                 +---------------------+                 |     PREPARE NODE    |                 |---------------------|                 | validate            |                 | clean               |                 | standardize         |                 | quarantine          |                 | account             |                 | revalidate          |                 | lineage             |                 +----------+----------+                            |                 prepared package                            |                            v                     FEATURE ENGINEERING                            |                            v                       SPLIT / TRAIN                            |                            v                         EVALUATE

PREPARE is the first place where the Brain's decisions touch the actual dataset. It is therefore the boundary between planning and execution. Its responsibility is to ensure that the data entering FE/STEM is not merely 'clean', but demonstrably compatible with the selected workflow, policy-compliant, traceable and reproducible.

For AI-ConneX, the correct mental model is: the Brain decides; PREPARE proves and prepares; FE transforms information into predictive signals; STEM learns and evaluates. This separation makes the pipeline easier to audit, debug, reproduce and adapt to industrial environments.
