sections.heading_text: Chapter 11: Data Studio FEATURE ENGINEER Node Detailed Documentation
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 11: Data Studio FEATURE ENGINEER Node Detailed Documentation
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

DATA STUDIO — FEATURE ENGINEER NODE

Industrial Intent-Driven Feature Engineering, Feature Registry & Deployment Bridge

Compliance Report #5 — Feature Engineering Stage

Figure 11.1: Feature Engineer Node Component Block

The Feature Engineer (FE) Node is the transformation intelligence layer immediately after PREPARE. PREPARE makes industrial data valid and execution-ready; FE converts that prepared data into meaningful, model-consumable features according to the user's intent, the Data Profiler's metadata, the selected DAG and the Recipe Orchestrator's feature-engineering plan.

AI-ConneX FE follows a registry-first strategy: if a validated feature recipe already exists and is compatible, the system reuses it. If no suitable recipe exists, an Agent Helper proposes a new recipe, but the generated recipe is not trusted merely because an agent produced it. It must pass schema, semantic, leakage, computational and reproducibility gates before execution.

CHATBOT INTENT      |      vAI-CONNEX BRAIN Compiler -> Profiler -> DAG -> Recipe Orchestrator      |      vPREPARE      |      | prepared dataset + manifest + profile + intent      v+-----------------------------+|      FEATURE ENGINEER       ||-----------------------------|| Intent Resolver             || Feature Registry            || Recipe Selector             || Agent Helper                || Leakage Guard               || Feature Validator           || Feature Lineage             |+--------------+--------------+               |       +-------+--------+       |                |       v                v   NEXT STUDIO       DEPLOYMENT   / STEM             BRIDGE

The purpose of FE is not to generate as many columns as possible. Its purpose is to generate the smallest useful, explainable, reproducible and deployment-compatible feature set that answers the industrial user's objective.

Figure 11.2: Data Studio Pipeline Context — Chatbot -> Brain -> PREPARE -> FE

Translate business intent into feature requirements.

Use Data Profiler metadata to understand available entities, timestamps, target, distributions and relationships.

Select an existing approved feature recipe whenever possible.

Ask an agent to design a candidate recipe when no suitable recipe exists.

Validate candidate features before execution.

Prevent temporal, target and cross-entity leakage.

Create reusable feature definitions and versions.

Maintain offline/online consistency when deployment requires serving features.

Produce a feature dataset, feature manifest and Compliance Report #5.

sections.heading_text: 3. Why FE Is Different from PREPARE
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 3. Why FE Is Different from PREPARE
sections.content: Example: converting pressure from psi to kPa belongs in PREPARE. A 15-minute rolling pressure mean, pressure trend and pressure-change rate belong in FE.

FE INPUT PACKAGE  prepared_dataset.parquet  prepared_manifest.json  manifest-UID.json  profile.json / profile reference  intent.json  dag_plan.json  feature_recipe_plan.json  lineage.json  policy bundle

The chatbot is the source of business intent, but FE does not directly execute natural-language instructions. The Brain converts intent into structured metadata and constraints. PREPARE validates the dataset. FE then uses the structured intent together with the observed profile.

USER:"Predict pump failure 6 hours in advance using sensor data."CHATBOT intent_uid objective = predictive maintenance entity = pump_id target = failure_event horizon = 6h explainability = required        |        vBRAIN / MANIFEST target semantics entity/time semantics available signals DAG recipe requirements        |        vPREPARE valid timestamp/entity/sensor data        |        vFEATURE ENGINEER lag / rolling / trend / rate-of-change features within the 6h prediction boundary

Figure 11.3: Incoming PREPARE Package Feeding Feature Engineering

The FE Intent Resolver converts structured intent into feature requirements. It should not invent business meaning.

feature_intent:  objective: predictive_maintenance  target: failure_event  horizon: 6h  entity_key: pump_id  event_time: timestamp  requirements:    temporal_features: true    rolling_windows: [15m, 1h, 6h, 24h]    explainability: required    online_serving: false  constraints:    no_future_data: true    no_target_derived_features: true    preserve_feature_lineage: true

The registry is the first-choice source of engineering logic. Reuse is preferred because a registered recipe has already been tested, versioned and associated with known schemas/tasks.

feature_registry/  recipes/    predictive_maintenance/      sensor_lag_v1.yaml      rolling_statistics_v2.yaml      degradation_trend_v1.yaml    demand_forecast/      lag_calendar_v1.yaml      rolling_demand_v2.yaml    anomaly_detection/      robust_stats_v1.yaml  metadata/  tests/  compatibility/

A recipe should declare its inputs, outputs, entity/time requirements, parameters, leakage assumptions, compute cost, serving mode and tests.

Intent  +Profile  +DAG  +Prepared Schema  |  vRecipe Compatibility Engine  |  +--> compatible approved recipe --> execute  |  +--> no compatible recipe --------> Agent Helper                                      |                                      v                                  candidate recipe                                      |                                      v                              validation gates                                      |                              +-------+-------+                              |               |                            reject          approve                                              |                                              v                                           execute

The Agent Helper is a controlled design assistant, not an unrestricted code generator. It can reason over the manifest, profile, intent, approved feature primitives and recipe examples to propose candidate feature definitions.

Suggest candidate features.

Explain why each feature is relevant.

Select approved primitives.

Generate a declarative recipe rather than arbitrary executable code where possible.

Identify required windows, keys and timestamps.

Flag uncertainty.

Request human/domain approval for ambiguous industrial semantics.

Agent-generated features must pass deterministic validation. An LLM/agent should never be the final authority for leakage safety or physical validity.

Industrial time-series problems require strict temporal semantics. A feature at event time t must use information available no later than the feature's permitted observation time. Point-in-time feature retrieval is a well-established approach for preventing future values from entering historical training data; Feast documents this explicitly for historical feature joins. citeturn0search0turn0search2

For target at t + 6h:allowed:  sensor(t)  sensor(t-5m)  rolling_mean(t-1h)  maintenance_state known by tnot allowed:  sensor(t+10m)  maintenance_state recorded at t+2h  future aggregate containing t+1h...t+6h

For temporal features, FE should maintain an entity key plus event timestamp and define an explicit lookback window/TTL. Feature stores such as Feast implement historical retrieval using event timestamps and point-in-time joins; this is useful as a reference architecture even if AI-ConneX implements its own registry/execution layer. citeturn0search0turn0search7

raw_sensor   |   +--> lag_5m   |   +--> rolling_mean_1h            |            +--> trend_1h                    |                    +--> degradation_score

Every feature should have a dependency graph. This makes it possible to identify target-derived features, future dependencies and redundant computation.

Data leakage is one of the most important FE risks. scikit-learn explicitly warns that transformations learned using test data can produce optimistic results and recommends fitting transformations only on training data while applying the same learned transformation to later data. citeturn0search1

Check feature timestamps against prediction timestamp.

Track dependency timestamps through feature graphs.

Prevent target-derived columns.

Prevent post-outcome operational fields.

Prevent train/test contamination.

Separate feature fitting from feature transformation where parameters are learned.

Use point-in-time joins for historical features.
Learned transformations should be fitted only in the appropriate training scope. The FE recipe must record whether a feature is deterministic or learned.

FE may produce candidate features, but feature selection should be controlled by the DAG and downstream modeling stage. Selection methods can include variance filtering, correlation redundancy, mutual information, model-based importance and domain rules.

Selection must be evaluated without leaking evaluation data. A feature with high apparent importance because it contains future information is a failure, not a successful feature.

Agentic systems can create thousands of technically valid features from every sensor/window combination. This increases compute cost, multicollinearity, model complexity and deployment latency.

Feature budget per recipe.

Maximum window count.

Maximum generated columns.

Duplicate/redundancy detection.

Compute-cost estimation before execution.

Importance-based pruning where justified.

Human approval for unusually large feature sets.

The strongest industrial features are often domain-aware rather than generic. AI-ConneX should support registered domain primitives such as equipment operating-state transitions, utilization, load-adjusted measurements, degradation indicators, maintenance intervals and engineering ratios.

The system should distinguish an approved engineering formula from an agent's speculative formula. Domain formulas should carry provenance and owner information.

Feature engineering often requires joins between telemetry, maintenance, production, quality and contextual datasets. These joins are high-risk because cardinality errors and temporal leakage can silently create incorrect features.

Validate entity keys.

Validate join cardinality.

Validate event timestamps.

Use point-in-time joins for historical context.

Record source feature view/table.

Record unmatched rows.

Record multiplicative row expansion.

Reject unexpected many-to-many joins.

For systems that require both historical training and online inference, a feature-store pattern is useful. Feast, for example, provides offline historical retrieval and online feature availability, with point-in-time correctness as a core concept. citeturn0search3turn0search5

AI-ConneX does not have to depend on Feast; the architectural requirement is a versioned feature registry plus reproducible offline/online definitions.

OFFLINEhistorical dataset     |feature recipe     |training featuresONLINElive event     |same feature definition     |serving features

The same logical feature definition should be used for training and inference. scikit-learn similarly emphasizes applying the same preprocessing transformation to test and production data as was applied during training. citeturn0search1

<domain>__<entity>__<signal>__<operation>__<window>__<version>sensor__pump__pressure__mean__1h__v2sensor__pump__temperature__delta__15m__v1maintenance__pump__hours_since_service__v1production__line__load_ratio__v3

Names should be stable, machine-readable and human interpretable. The registry remains the authoritative definition.

feature:  id: FEAT-000142  name: sensor__pump__pressure__mean__1h__v2  version: 2.0.0  entity:    key: pump_id    timestamp: event_timestamp  inputs:    - pressure_kpa  operation:    type: rolling_mean    window: 1h    min_periods: 3  availability:    max_lag: 0    online: false  leakage:    point_in_time: required  lineage:    source_dataset_uid: ACX-DATA-00042    recipe_id: FEAT-RCP-009

sections.heading_text: 26. What FE Sends to the Next Studio
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 26. What FE Sends to the Next Studio
sections.content:
If the selected DAG indicates another Studio component, FE publishes a versioned feature package rather than just a file.

feature_package/  feature_dataset.parquet  feature_manifest.json  feature_schema.json  feature_recipe.json  feature_lineage.json  feature_validation.json  feature_report_5.json  target_definition.json

The receiving Studio validates the package against the manifest and schema before consumption.

Direct deployment should only be permitted when the DAG and intent explicitly select an inference/serving path and all deployment gates pass. FE should never independently decide to deploy simply because features were successfully generated.

FE | +--> next Studio / STEM | +--> batch scoring | +--> online feature serving | +--> deployment gateway       |       +--> security gate       +--> model compatibility       +--> feature availability       +--> latency/cost       +--> approval

Examples include maintenance completion codes entered after a failure, future production totals, post-failure inspection fields and labels accidentally included in rolling aggregates. AI-ConneX builds a target dependency graph and marks target/post-outcome fields as restricted.

target: failure_eventRESTRICTED  failure_confirmed  repair_completed  post_failure_inspectionALLOWED BEFORE t  vibration(t)  temperature(t)  pressure(t-1h)  operating_load(t)

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 31. Failure: Temporal Leakage Through Aggregation
sections.content: A common mistake is computing a daily aggregate over the complete day and attaching it to every row in that day. For a 10:00 prediction, the 18:00 measurement must not influence the feature. AI-ConneX requires window definitions to be anchored at the event time.

Generated code should not have unrestricted filesystem, network or shell access. The preferred architecture is declarative recipes built from allowlisted feature primitives. If code generation is unavoidable, execution should occur in an isolated sandbox with resource limits and explicit permissions.

A feature named 'temperature trend' may mean different things across industries. AI-ConneX stores the operation definition, units, entity, time window and semantic description rather than relying on a name alone.

Cardinality validation.

Temporal availability validation.

Constant/near-constant detection.

Distribution sanity checks.

Serving compatibility validation.

RQ1: Does registry-first feature reuse reduce feature engineering time?

RQ2: Does agent-assisted recipe generation increase useful feature coverage without increasing leakage?

sections.content:
AI-ConneX

DATA STUDIO — IF/ELSE CONDITIONING & INDUSTRIAL VISUALIZATION DEPLOYMENT GATE

Post–Feature Engineer Decision Node | Compliance Report #6

The AI-ConneX IF/ELSE Conditioning Node is the controlled decision gate immediately after Feature Engineer (FE). Its job is not to perform another generic transformation. It determines what the user actually wants to do with the engineered data: deploy it as an industrial Data Studio Microservice/Service for organization, mathematical/physics-aware analysis and visualization, or route the workflow to ML Studio when the intent is explicitly model-oriented.

CHATBOT INTENT      |      vBRAIN Compiler -> Profiler -> DAG -> Recipe Orchestrator      |      vPREPARE      |      vFEATURE ENGINEER      |      v+--------------------------------+| IF / ELSE CONDITIONING NODE    ||                                || IF intent = DATA/SERVICE       ||       -> DEPLOYMENT NODE       ||       -> Physics/Math Layer    ||       -> Visualization Service ||                                || ELSE IF intent = MODEL/ML      ||       -> ML STUDIO             ||                                || ELSE                           ||       -> clarification/gate    |+--------------------------------+

Figure 12.1: Destination ML Studio Pipeline Architecture

The architectural principle is: **do not force an ML model where a deterministic mathematical/physics visualization service already solves the industrial problem.** Many industrial users need better organization, monitoring, signal interpretation, derived measurements, engineering views, anomaly marking, and interactive visualization rather than prediction.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 2. Why This Decision Node Exists
sections.content:
Feature engineering can produce a useful analytical representation even when no machine-learning model is required. An industrialist may want to visualize vibration spectra, compare machine cycles, inspect pressure/flow relationships, monitor energy consumption, detect threshold violations, calculate FFT/PSD, overlay engineering limits, or explore process behavior. These tasks can be delivered as deterministic services.

Conversely, if the user's intent is predictive, classificatory, forecasting, recommendation-oriented or explicitly model-driven, the engineered feature package should go to ML Studio rather than being silently converted into a visualization service.

IF user_intent.requires_model == TRUE:       route = ML_STUDIOELSE IF user_intent.requires_service == TRUE     OR user_intent.requires_visualization == TRUE     OR user_intent.requires_analysis == TRUE:       route = DEPLOYMENT_NODEELSE:       route = CLARIFICATION_GATE

Figure 12.2: Direct Intent Route — Chatbot to Split Node in ML Studio

The actual implementation should use a structured intent contract from the Brain rather than parsing raw chatbot text at this late stage.

sections.content:
Deployment here does not necessarily mean deploying an ML model. It means exposing a reusable industrial data service. The service can accept data, calculate deterministic mathematical/physics-derived quantities, organize them into views, and return interactive or machine-readable outputs.

For vibration, acoustic, electrical and rotating-equipment datasets, an FFT-based service can transform a time-domain signal into a frequency-domain representation. The service can mark frequency peaks, harmonics, configured bands and engineering reference regions.

sections.heading_text: 33. Why the IF/ELSE Node Must Not Be an Agent-Only Decision
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 33. Why the IF/ELSE Node Must Not Be an Agent-Only Decision
sections.content:
An agent can interpret intent, but a deterministic policy engine should make the final route. This is important because the route has operational consequences: ML Studio may create a training lifecycle, while Deployment may expose a service. The system should not allow probabilistic language interpretation alone to choose a production path.

Agent interpretation        |        vStructured intent        |        vDeterministic policy engine        |    +---+---+    |       |  ML      SERVICE

Figure 12.3: ML Studio Internal Loop — Split Node to Train Node

Where natural-language intent is ambiguous, the system should not guess. For example, 'show me whether the pump will fail' could mean a visualization of historical failures or a predictive model. The gate should request clarification or use an explicit Brain-level intent contract.

sections.heading_text: 35. Why Not Deploy Directly After PREPARE?
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 35. Why Not Deploy Directly After PREPARE?
sections.content: Because FE may create the exact derived signals required for useful visualization or downstream model input. If deployment happens before FE, later feature definitions can diverge between analytical and deployed paths. FE provides the stable analytical contract that both branches can consume.

sections.heading_text: 36. Why Not Put the Gate After ML Studio?
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 36. Why Not Put the Gate After ML Studio?
sections.content:
That would be architecturally wrong because ML Studio is itself a downstream specialization. The purpose of the gate is to choose whether ML Studio is needed. Sending every workload into ML first introduces unnecessary training, evaluation, model governance and maintenance overhead.

Figure 12.4: ML Studio Internal Loop — Train Node to Evaluation Metrics

sections.heading_text: 37. Why Not Put the Gate in the Brain?
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 37. Why Not Put the Gate in the Brain?
sections.content: The Brain should understand and plan the workflow, and it may propose the route. However, the final routing gate belongs after FE because the system now has the final feature package and can verify that the requested service/model path is technically possible. This creates a defense-in-depth architecture: Brain plans; the post-FE gate validates and commits the route.

def route(ctx):    if not ctx.fe_report.pass_status:        return BLOCK    if ctx.intent.requires_model:        return ML_STUDIO    if (        ctx.intent.requires_service        or ctx.intent.requires_visualization        or ctx.intent.requires_analysis    ):        return DEPLOYMENT    return CLARIFICATION

Production implementation should also include policy, security, resource and compatibility checks.

FE Compliance Report #5 is PASS.

The mathematical layer must validate numerical assumptions. For FFT, for example, the sampling rate determines the frequency axis. If the sampling frequency is missing or inconsistent, the system should block or explicitly mark the result as invalid rather than producing a visually convincing but incorrect spectrum.

Sampling-rate validation.

Physics-derived outputs require stricter controls than generic mathematics because a formula can be mathematically valid but physically inappropriate.

sections.heading_text: 54. Failure: Visualization That Looks Correct but Is Wrong
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 54. Failure: Visualization That Looks Correct but Is Wrong
sections.content: A major industrial risk is a visually attractive chart built from incorrect sampling, units, timestamps or aggregation. AI-ConneX therefore treats visualization as an analytical result requiring contracts and validation, not as a cosmetic frontend operation.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 55. Failure: Physics Formula Without Units
sections.content: For example, adding pressure in bar to pressure in psi is numerically possible but physically meaningless. The Physics Layer must require compatible units before calculation. Where unit conversion is needed, the conversion should be explicit and lineage-tracked.

An agent can generate dozens of charts that overwhelm operators. AI-ConneX should optimize for task relevance: the user's intent plus profiler metadata determine the minimum useful set of visualizations.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 57. Failure: Service vs Model Confusion
sections.content: A deterministic threshold visualization should not be marketed as AI prediction. Conversely, if the user explicitly asks for a failure probability, the system must route to ML Studio. Clear separation improves governance, explainability and lifecycle management.

The IF/ELSE Conditioning Node is the architectural point where AI-ConneX decides whether the engineered data should become a model input or an industrial analytical service. It prevents the system from over-engineering simple problems with ML while ensuring genuine model requests are not weakened into visualization-only services.

The governing rule is: **If the industrial problem can be solved deterministically and the user wants organization, analysis or visualization, deploy a governed Data Studio service. If the user needs prediction, classification, forecasting, optimization or another learned model, route to ML Studio. If the intent is ambiguous, ask rather than guess.**

sections.heading_text: Chapter 13: Data Studio VISUAL INTELLIGENCE AGENT LAYER Linked Architecture
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 13: Data Studio VISUAL INTELLIGENCE AGENT LAYER Linked Architecture
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

DATA STUDIO — VISUAL INTELLIGENCE & AGENT LAYER

Shared Mathematical Visualization Foundation for Data Profiler, DAG Assigner, Recipe Orchestrator and Decision Services

This document adds an architectural layer that was intentionally not separated in the earlier stage documents: Data Visualisation is not only a final-user interface in AI-ConneX. It is also an internal reasoning instrument used by the Data Profiler, DAG Assigner and Agent Working Layer to understand the dataset mathematically and make better decisions.

The goal is to make this addition explicit without changing the existing stage boundaries. Visualization is a shared evidence layer; it does not replace profiling, DAG assignment, feature engineering or the final deployment visualization service.

This document should therefore be read as a cross-cutting architecture document linked to the Compiler → Data Profiler → DAG → Recipe Orchestrator → PREPARE → Feature Engineer → IF/ELSE → ML Studio/Deployment pipeline.

AI-ConneX uses two different meanings of visualization, and they must not be confused.

Both can use the same mathematical primitives and rendering technology, but their governance, audience and lifecycle are different.

sections.heading_text: 3. Where the Visual Intelligence Layer Fits
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 3. Where the Visual Intelligence Layer Fits
sections.content:
AI-CONNEX DATA STUDIOUSER | vCHATBOT | v+---------------- BRAIN ----------------+|                                        || Compiler                               ||    |                                   ||    v                                   || Data Profiler <---- Visual Evidence ---+|    |                    ^              ||    v                    |              || DAG Assigner <----------+              ||    |                    |              ||    v                    |              || Recipe Orchestrator <---+              ||                                        || Agent Working Layer -------------------++----------------------------------------+ | vPREPARE | vFEATURE ENGINEER | vIF/ELSE |                 | v                 vML STUDIO       DEPLOYMENT                   |                   v          User-facing Math/Physics          Visualization Service

Figure 13.2: JANE Chatbot Interface to The Brain in Visual Intelligence Context

The Visual Intelligence Layer runs alongside the reasoning stages. It receives data/metadata snapshots and produces mathematical evidence, charts, distributions, correlations, time-series summaries and other diagnostics that agents and deterministic decision engines can consume.

sections.heading_text: 4. The Agent Is the Reasoning Base
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 4. The Agent Is the Reasoning Base
sections.content:
The Agent Working Layer is the intelligent interpretation layer that uses structured metadata plus visual evidence. It should not be allowed to directly modify the dataset merely because a chart looks unusual. Instead, it proposes interpretations and actions that deterministic validators and stage-specific policies approve.

Dataset  |  +--> Profile metadata  |  +--> Mathematical evidence  |  +--> Visual evidence          |          v       AGENT          |    interpretation          |          v deterministic validators          |          v stage decision

Figure 13.3: JANE Chatbot as Reasoning Base Icon

This is particularly important for industrial data because distributions, correlations and time-series plots often reveal structure that is difficult to capture through schema metadata alone.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 5. Why Visual Evidence Is Needed
sections.content:
Schema alone cannot reveal skew, multimodality or outliers.

Column names alone cannot reveal whether a variable is time-dependent.

Data types alone cannot reveal seasonality or drift.

Null counts alone cannot reveal sensor dropouts or operating-state gaps.

Correlation tables alone can hide nonlinear or regime-specific relationships.

Aggregates alone can hide cycle-level behavior.

Visual inspection can reveal patterns that guide the next analytical operation.

The visual layer converts mathematical summaries into evidence that both humans and agents can inspect.

The Data Profiler remains responsible for assigning the dataset profile. The visual layer supplies additional evidence to that profiling process.

Compiler Output      |      vData Profiler  |  +--> schema profile  +--> statistical profile  +--> semantic profile  +--> quality profile  +--> VISUAL EVIDENCE          |          +--> histograms          +--> box plots          +--> missingness maps          +--> time-series plots          +--> correlation matrices          +--> distributions          +--> cardinality views          +--> sampling diagnostics  |  vmanifest-UID.json

sections.heading_text: 7. What the Data Profiler Learns from Visualization
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 7. What the Data Profiler Learns from Visualization
sections.content: These are evidence-based candidates, not automatic truths. The Profiler should record confidence and validation status.

The visual layer is backed by a Mathematical Reference Engine. This engine produces numeric summaries first and visualizations second. This distinction is important: the chart is a representation of an analytical result, not the source of truth.

raw/feature data      |      vMathematical Reference Engine      |      +--> count      +--> mean      +--> std      +--> quantiles      +--> entropy/cardinality      +--> correlation      +--> autocorrelation      +--> frequency analysis      +--> missingness      +--> temporal regularity      |      vEvidence objects      |      +--> machine-readable JSON      +--> visualization specifications      +--> rendered charts

{  "evidence_uid": "ACX-VIZ-EV-00017",  "dataset_uid": "ACX-DATA-00042",  "stage": "DATA_PROFILER",  "type": "distribution",  "column": "pressure_bar",  "statistics": {    "count": 98120,    "mean": 5.42,    "std": 0.61,    "p01": 4.01,    "p99": 6.83  },  "visualization": {    "type": "histogram"  },  "source_snapshot": "sha256:...",  "confidence": 0.98}

Evidence objects provide a stable machine-readable bridge between visualization and agent reasoning.

sections.heading_text: 10. Visualization Does NOT Become the Profile
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 10. Visualization Does NOT Become the Profile
sections.content:
The chart itself should not be embedded as the semantic profile. The Data Profiler owns the profile and manifest. Visualization produces evidence referenced by the profile.

WRONG:Chart -> becomes ProfileCORRECT:Data -> Profile     -> Mathematical Evidence     -> Visual Evidence             |             v       Profile Decision             |             v       manifest-UID.json

The DAG Assigner uses the Profiler's profile to identify valid data flows and possible analytical tasks. Visual evidence can make this process more reliable by showing whether columns behave as time, categorical, entity, target, sensor or derived variables.

Profiler   |   +--> profile   +--> visual evidence          |          v      DAG Assigner          |          +--> entity relationships          +--> temporal dependencies          +--> candidate transformations          +--> aggregation opportunities          +--> join risks          +--> DAG candidates

sections.heading_text: 12. How Visual Evidence Helps DAG Decisions
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 12. How Visual Evidence Helps DAG Decisions
sections.content: The DAG should never be inferred solely from a visual chart. Visual evidence is one signal combined with schema, metadata, keys, lineage, constraints and deterministic validation.

Data lineage graph.

Column dependency graph.

Entity relationship graph.

Temporal dependency graph.

Join-key coverage matrix.

Missingness-by-table matrix.

Transformation dependency graph.

Candidate pipeline graph.

Feature-to-source dependency graph.

These are decision visualizations rather than end-user dashboards.

Chatbot-derived user intent.

Compiler output.

Profiler metadata.

Visual evidence objects.

Existing recipes.

DAG constraints.

Domain knowledge.

Industrial vocabulary.

Policy and compliance rules.

Previous stage reports.
All agent outputs must remain explicitly labeled as proposals until deterministic or domain validation accepts them.

Suppose a factory dataset contains `timestamp`, `machine_id`, `vibration`, `temperature` and `pressure`. The agent sees a time-series plot where vibration has strong periodic behavior and a distribution with several modes.

Agent observation:  "vibration exhibits periodic structure and multiple regimes."Evidence:  autocorrelation peak  frequency-domain peak  multimodal distributionCandidate recommendation:  "Treat as time-series sensor data;   consider FFT and operating-state segmentation."Validator:  timestamp ordering = PASS  sampling regularity = PASS  sufficient observations = PASSAccepted profile enrichment:  temporal_sensor = true
Agent confidence should not be treated as statistical certainty. AI-ConneX should distinguish between computational confidence and model/agent confidence.

sections.heading_text: 20. Relationship to the Previous IF/ELSE Document
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 20. Relationship to the Previous IF/ELSE Document
sections.content:
The IF/ELSE stage described previously remains unchanged. This document explains the earlier cross-cutting capability that also supports that stage.

VISUAL INTELLIGENCE       |       +--> Data Profiler       +--> DAG Assigner       +--> Recipe Orchestrator       +--> Agent Working Layer       |       +--> FE diagnostics       |       +--> IF/ELSE evidence       |       +--> Deployment visualization

The important distinction is that the same mathematical foundation can be reused, but each stage consumes it for a different purpose.

The Compiler's job remains dataset normalization: unzip, parse, join, append, merge, convert formats and produce a unified representation. The visual layer can be used after compilation to inspect whether the unified dataset behaves as expected.

Compare row counts before/after merge.

Compare column distributions.

Visualize duplicate keys.

Inspect missingness introduced by joins.

Check timestamp continuity.

Compare source-table ranges.

The Recipe Orchestrator can use visual evidence to select or validate recipes. For example, a highly skewed numerical feature may support a transformation candidate; a time-series plot may indicate that temporal splitting is required.

However, the Recipe Orchestrator remains responsible for recipe selection and linkage to the manifest. Visualization only supplies evidence.

PREPARE can consume visual evidence to validate that cleaning operations had the intended effect.

Before PREPARE  missingness = 18%  duplicates = 3.2%After PREPARE  missingness = 0.4%  duplicates = 0%Visual evidence:  before/after distributions  missingness map  timestamp continuity

FE can use visual diagnostics to validate engineered features. For example, a lag feature should show temporal alignment, while rolling features should not introduce unexpected leakage or edge artifacts.

Feature distributions.

Feature-target relationships.

Temporal alignment.

Outlier behavior.

Correlation/redundancy.

Feature cardinality.

Windowing effects.

The IF/ELSE gate can use evidence to validate that a deterministic service is technically appropriate. For example, if the user requests FFT visualization, the evidence layer can verify sampling information and signal characteristics before the Deployment Node is allowed to publish the service.

Agent never treats a visualization as proof by itself.

Agent never changes source data during observation.

Agent proposals must be reproducible.

Input: industrial sensor dataset. The Profiler generates numerical statistics plus histogram, missingness map, time-series plot and correlation view. The Agent sees the evidence and proposes `time_series_sensor=true`. The deterministic Profiler validator checks timestamp ordering and sampling regularity before enriching the profile.

The DAG Assigner receives the profile and evidence. A temporal plot indicates that sensor measurements depend on timestamp and machine ID. Join coverage shows machine IDs are shared across two tables. The DAG candidate therefore proposes entity/time alignment before aggregation.

TABLE A: machine_eventsmachine_id -> timestamp -> eventTABLE B: sensor_valuesmachine_id -> timestamp -> measurementVisual evidence:  timestamp regularity  key coverage  entity distributionsDAG candidate:  align -> join -> validate -> aggregate

The Agent is given intent + profile + evidence. It proposes a recipe or DAG candidate but does not execute it until validators approve the proposal.

Observation -> Hypothesis -> Proposal -> Validation -> Acceptance    ^                                      |    |--------------------------------------|             feedback/evidence

CHATBOT INTENT      |COMPILER      |DATA PROFILER  |         |        VISUAL EVIDENCE  |             |  v             vPROFILE ------> AGENT  |             |  +------> DAG |             |             v       RECIPE ORCHESTRATOR             |             v          PREPARE             |             v      FEATURE ENGINEER             |             v         IF / ELSE        /                v           v  ML STUDIO    DEPLOYMENT                   |                   v          User Visualization
The Visual Intelligence Layer needs its own evidence governance even though it is cross-cutting.

Can visual evidence improve automated industrial dataset profiling?

Does evidence-aware Agent reasoning reduce incorrect DAG candidates?

Which visual summaries provide the highest decision value per compute cost?

Can machine-readable evidence improve reproducibility of Agent decisions?

Does separating evidence from profile reduce hallucination risk?

Can a shared mathematical registry support both internal reasoning and deployed visualization?

H1: Visual evidence improves classification of industrial datasets into temporal, relational and analytical profiles.

H2: DAG candidates generated with visual evidence require fewer manual corrections.

H3: Registry-based mathematical evidence reduces agent-generated analytical inconsistencies.

H4: Evidence-linked agent proposals provide stronger auditability than free-form agent reasoning.

Cooley, J. W., & Tukey, J. W. (1965). An Algorithm for the Machine Calculation of Complex Fourier Series. Mathematics of Computation, 19(90), 297–301.

Welch, P. D. (1967). The Use of Fast Fourier Transform for the Estimation of Power Spectra. IEEE Transactions on Audio and Electroacoustics, 15(2), 70–73.

Tukey, J. W. (1977). Exploratory Data Analysis. Addison-Wesley. Foundational reference for exploratory statistical visualization.

Wilkinson, L. (2005). The Grammar of Graphics. Springer. Foundation for structured visualization specifications.

Munzner, T. (2014). Visualization Analysis and Design. CRC Press. Reference for visualization design and analytical reasoning.

Apache Arrow documentation. Columnar data representation and interoperability.

NumPy documentation. Numerical computation.

SciPy documentation. Scientific and signal-processing computation.

Plotly documentation. Interactive analytical visualization.

These references support the mathematical, exploratory-analysis and visualization foundations. Industrial/domain decisions should additionally be validated against sector-specific engineering standards and peer-reviewed literature.

The missing architectural concept is therefore not 'another visualization module'. It is a **Visual Intelligence & Agent Evidence Layer** that connects the mathematical reality of the dataset to AI-ConneX's reasoning stages.

DATA | +--> numeric evidence +--> visual evidence +--> metadata        |        v      AGENT        |        v PROFILER / DAG / RECIPES        |        v  governed pipeline        |        v final user-facing visualization

The key distinction is: **visualization is an evidence mechanism throughout the pipeline, and a product/service interface at the end.** The mathematical foundation can be shared, while stage-specific contracts prevent ambiguity.

sections.heading_text: 48. Reader Navigation — How to Read AI-ConneX Documents
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 48. Reader Navigation — How to Read AI-ConneX Documents
sections.content: This document is intentionally cross-cutting and should be referenced from the Data Profiler, DAG, Recipe Orchestrator, Feature Engineer and IF/ELSE documentation rather than replacing those documents.

AI-ConneX's differentiator is not merely that it can visualize industrial data. Its stronger architectural proposition is that mathematical visualization becomes part of the system's reasoning loop: the Compiler establishes a unified representation; the Profiler creates structured metadata and visual evidence; the DAG uses evidence to construct valid workflow candidates; the Recipe Orchestrator uses it for recipe selection/validation; PREPARE and FE use it for quality/feature diagnostics; and the IF/ELSE stage can finally expose the same analytical capabilities as a governed industrial service.

The Agent is the interpretation layer over this evidence, while deterministic engines, registries, validation and lineage remain the control mechanisms. This separation makes AI-ConneX more explainable, reproducible and suitable for industrial environments.

TAS | AI-ConneX — Data Studio VISUAL INTELLIGENCE AGENT LAYER Linked Architecture End-of-Stage Verification

sections.heading_text: Chapter 14: ML Studio STEM One Loop IF ELSE Documentation
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 14: ML Studio STEM One Loop IF ELSE Documentation
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

ML STUDIO — S.T.E.M.

Split • Train • Evaluate Metrics • Judge • Score • DeliverOne-Loop Multi-DAG / Multi-Family Architecture

Figure 14.1: ML Studio S.T.E.M. Execution Topology

ML Studio is the model-building execution environment of AI-ConneX. It is entered either from a new user intent through Jane or from Data Studio after industrial data has been prepared and feature-engineered. In both paths Jane discusses and confirms the model-building plan before expensive execution.

When Data Studio supplies the input, ML Studio receives a standard STEM recipe template covering Split, Train and Evaluate Metrics. When ML Studio is invoked independently as a microservice, Jane first runs a clean-validator. If the data is not sufficiently prepared, Jane explains the missing steps and recommends Data Studio. If it is clean, ML Studio creates a new manifest and invokes the DAG Assigner and Recipe Orchestrator once to obtain candidate DAG IDs, Family IDs and STEM recipes.

The core is a one-loop experiment: for every suggested DAG and Family ID, the system performs the approved split, trains all suggested models, evaluates all models with declared metrics, and then uses Judge and Scorer Agents to select the best acceptable model with reasons.

USER | vJANE | | +--> new intent --------------------+ |                                     | +--> Data Studio ---------------------+                                       v                                MODEL PLAN                                       |                         +-------------+-------------+                         |                           |                  STEM ONE-LOOP               NO ACCEPTABLE                         |                     MODEL PATH             DAG x FAMILY x MODEL                         |                Split -> Train -> Evaluate                         |                  Judge + Scorer                         |                         v                 Best Model + Reasons

ML Studio is not a replacement for Data Studio. Data Studio makes industrial data understandable and model-ready; ML Studio performs controlled model experimentation, comparison and selection.

Jane is the conversational control plane. Natural-language intent becomes an explicit Model Plan before training.

Business objective

User Intent -> Jane -> clarify -> ModelPlan -> user confirmation -> STEM

External dataset      |      vClean Validator   |          | FAIL       PASS   |          | Jane       new ML manifest explains     | missing      +--> DAG + Recipe Orchestrator steps              (ONE bootstrap)   | recommend Data Studio

The validator is a safety boundary, not a second Data Studio. It checks whether the dataset is sufficiently ready for the declared model task.

ML Studio should not silently repair major data-quality problems and then train. The user is told what is missing and why Data Studio is recommended.

sections.heading_text: 10. Why DAG + Recipe Orchestrator Runs Once
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 10. Why DAG + Recipe Orchestrator Runs Once
sections.content:
Obtains the candidate execution plan.

Obtains Family IDs and STEM recipe references.

Freezes the experiment space.

Prevents plan regeneration during model comparison.

Improves reproducibility and auditability.

Reduces unnecessary agent/tool calls.

A material change in objective, data, split policy or feature definition creates a new plan/version rather than mutating the active experiment.
Judge and Scorer are downstream decision agents; they do not replace STEM evaluation.

for DAG in suggested_DAGs:    for FAMILY in suggested_Families:        SPLIT = stem.split(DATA, DAG, FAMILY)        for MODEL in FAMILY.suggested_models:            MODEL_ARTIFACT = stem.train(MODEL, SPLIT.train)            METRICS = stem.evaluate(MODEL_ARTIFACT,                                    SPLIT.validation,                                    SPLIT.test)            store(DAG, FAMILY, MODEL, METRICS)Judge(all_results)Scorer(all_results)Select(best_acceptable)

Implementation may execute candidates in parallel, but logically all candidates belong to one versioned experiment graph.
Different DAGs represent alternative valid transformations, dependencies, aggregation paths or temporal structures. Each candidate must remain separately identifiable.
Family IDs represent controlled candidate model families. The model registry determines which executable models belong to each family.

The split strategy is part of the experiment manifest. Comparable candidates must use a comparable declared split policy.

Fit preprocessing only on training data.

Keep future information out of training.

Respect entity boundaries.

Respect temporal boundaries.

Track feature provenance.

Check duplicate prediction units.

Validate target leakage before training.

Metrics are selected before results are seen and must reflect the industrial cost of errors.

{  "result_uid": "ACX-ML-RES-001",  "dag_id": "DAG-03",  "family_id": "FAM-02",  "model_id": "MODEL-17",  "split_uid": "SPLIT-09",  "metrics": {"mae": 0.184, "rmse": 0.271},  "evaluation_dataset": "test",  "artifact_hash": "sha256:..."}

Judge is the reasoned suitability layer. It compares validated candidates against the user objective and industrial constraints.

Scorer applies a versioned quantitative selection policy. It must not change weights after seeing results.

score =    w1 * primary_metric_score  + w2 * secondary_metric_score  + w3 * stability_score  + w4 * resource_score  + w5 * interpretability_score  - penalties

Weights, metric direction and penalty rules are configuration and are included in the experiment record.

sections.heading_text: Chapter 15: Agentic Studio Main Agent and Agentic Toolkit Documentation
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 15: Agentic Studio Main Agent and Agentic Toolkit Documentation
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

AGENTIC STUDIO — MAIN AGENT & AGENTIC TOOLKIT

R&D • Architecture • Runtime Integration • Industrial Operations • POC • Compliance Report #5Version 1.0 | 14 August 2026

Figure 15.1: Agentic Studio Master Architecture Diagram

The Main Agent and Agentic Toolkit are the operational outputs of Agentic Studio. The Main Agent is not another unrestricted chatbot: it is the industrial execution persona instantiated from an Agent SPEC and backed by Agent Runtime, RAG, Knowledge Graph, Knowledge Base, telemetry, evaluated models and governed tools. The Agentic Toolkit is the reusable capability layer that lets an industrial organization monitor assets, interpret state, create alerts, generate reports, investigate events, coordinate maintenance workflows and perform approved actions without requiring a dedicated data scientist or agent engineer for every routine.

The central separation is: Main Agent = accountable coordinator; Toolkit = reusable capabilities; Runtime = enforcement/execution engine; SPEC = contract; Knowledge Foundation = evidence; Policy = authorization; Visualizer = human operational view.

USER / INDUSTRIALIST        |      JANE        |    USER INTENT        |   AGENT BUILDER        |    AGENT SPEC        |  AGENT RUNTIME        |  +-----+-----------------------------+  | Knowledge / Models / Telemetry    |  |                                   |  +----------------+------------------+                   |             MAIN AGENT                   |        +----------+-----------+        |      AGENTIC TOOLKIT |        +----------+-----------+                   |       alerts / reports / workflows       diagnostics / monitoring       governed industrial actions                   |              OT/IT systems                   |             VISUALIZER                   |              OPERATOR

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 2. What Is the Main Agent?
sections.content:
The Main Agent is the single industrial-facing agent instance produced by Agentic Studio for a specific user, site, operational objective or managed industrial environment. It maintains the execution context, interprets current evidence, plans within the permitted action envelope, invokes toolkit capabilities, explains outcomes and escalates when evidence or authority is insufficient.

It is instantiated from a versioned Agent SPEC.

It never receives unrestricted tool access.

It uses the Knowledge Foundation for grounded evidence.

It uses telemetry for current operational state.

It may call evaluated ML Studio models through their contracts.

It delegates side effects to the Agentic Toolkit/Tool Gateway.

It records decisions, evidence, tool calls and outcomes.

It can operate in INFORM, RECOMMEND, APPROVE-THEN-ACT or configured AUTONOMOUS modes.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 3. What Is the Agentic Toolkit?
sections.content:
The Agentic Toolkit is the reusable capability catalog around the Main Agent. A toolkit capability is a typed, versioned operation with defined inputs, outputs, permissions, side effects, limits and observability. Toolkit capabilities can be composed into industrial workflows.

Toolkit capabilities are not all equal. Read-only operations can generally have lower autonomy requirements than actions that modify operational or business state.

A monolithic agent becomes difficult to govern because reasoning, knowledge access, permissions, integrations and side effects become inseparable. A toolkit makes capabilities explicit and testable. The Main Agent can then coordinate capabilities without owning every implementation detail.

Create an industrial agent that is useful without pretending to be a human engineer.

Convert complex industrial workflows into reusable capabilities.

Separate reasoning from authorization and side effects.

Provide evidence-backed explanations.

Operate with degraded capability when data, models or integrations fail.

Make every capability testable independently.

Support multi-site and multi-asset deployments without cross-scope leakage.

Allow industrialists to configure outcomes rather than implement agent code.

A constrained coordinator plus typed tools is safer than a monolithic autonomous agent.

Industrial utility improves when current telemetry, historical knowledge and asset topology are available together.

Explicit capability contracts reduce accidental side effects.

Evidence and action provenance improves operator trust and incident reconstruction.

Progressive autonomy is more appropriate for industrial deployment than unconditional autonomy.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 7. Previous Stage Input — Jane / Chatbot

sections.heading_text: 8. Agent SPEC as the Main Agent Contract
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 8. Agent SPEC as the Main Agent Contract
sections.content: The signed SPEC is authoritative. The Main Agent can select among permitted capabilities but cannot create permission through reasoning.

CREATE  -> LOAD SPEC  -> VERIFY SIGNATURE  -> RESOLVE SCOPE  -> INITIALIZE CONTEXT  -> OBSERVE  -> RETRIEVE  -> PLAN  -> PROPOSE  -> POLICY CHECK  -> TOOL EXECUTION  -> VERIFY RESULT  -> EXPLAIN  -> AUDIT  -> WAIT / MONITOR / ESCALATE

while execution_active:    observe()    context = gather_evidence(        rag=True, graph=True, telemetry=True    )    plan = reason_within_spec(context)    proposal = validate_plan(plan)    decision = policy.evaluate(proposal)    if decision == "DENY":        explain_and_audit()        break    if decision == "APPROVAL_REQUIRED":        request_human_approval()        continue    result = toolkit.execute(proposal)    verify(result)    update_state()    audit()

The model is therefore one component of the loop, not the security boundary.

{  "capability_uid": "CAP-ALERT-CREATE",  "version": "1.4.0",  "name": "create_alert",  "description": "Create a maintenance alert",  "input_schema": "ALERT-V3",  "output_schema": "ALERT-RESULT-V2",  "side_effect": "WRITE",  "risk_class": "OPERATIONAL",  "requires_approval": true,  "allowed_scopes": ["PLANT-01"],  "idempotency": "required",  "timeout_seconds": 20,  "audit_required": true}

MAIN AGENT                         |                  Capability Planner                         |                  Toolkit Registry                         |        +----------------+----------------+        |                |                |    Observe           Diagnose         Visualize        |                |                |      data             models           math/physics        |                |                |        +----------------+----------------+                         |                    Policy Gateway                         |                 Connector Adapters              /        |        |                   CMMS      MES      SCADA    ERP
The exact classification is site-specific. A 'write' to a maintenance system is not equivalent to a control command to a physical machine.

The Visualizer is a toolkit capability, not the Main Agent itself. It turns telemetry, mathematical transforms, model outputs and event markers into operator-readable views. Examples include FFT/spectrum analysis, time trends, envelope analysis, anomaly overlays, row/column marking and asset-state dashboards.

FFT for vibration/frequency-domain analysis.

Time-domain trend with detected events.

Spectrogram for changing frequency content.

Threshold and model-score overlays.

Per-row/per-column annotations for structured datasets.

Asset topology visualization from Knowledge Graph.

Evidence markers linking a visual event to telemetry/document/model provenance.

The visualizer should never imply that a mathematical transformation is a diagnosis. It displays computed evidence and model results with units, windows, timestamps and provenance.

Main Agent   |   +--> RAG: "What approved procedure applies?"   |   +--> KG: "What components/sensors are connected?"   |   +--> Telemetry: "What is happening now?"   |   +--> Model: "What does the evaluated model estimate?"   |   +--> Toolkit: "What bounded operation is allowed?"

This prevents the Main Agent from using a single source for every type of question.

OWASP defines excessive agency as damaging actions enabled by excessive functionality, permissions or autonomy. The Main Agent therefore does not receive a broad API surface and choose freely. The SPEC selects capabilities; policy checks each call; the gateway executes; and high-consequence operations can require approval. citeturn0search2

Agent decides WHAT it proposes        |SPEC decides WHAT exists        |Policy decides WHETHER it is allowed        |Gateway decides HOW it executes        |Audit records WHAT happened
The toolkit must not be used to bypass PLC/SCADA safety systems or site safety procedures.

AI-ConneX should normally operate above the industrial control safety layer. The Main Agent can monitor and recommend; where a control integration exists, the interface must enforce an independent safety and authorization boundary. Agentic AI should not be treated as a substitute for SIS, interlocks, PLC safety logic or validated control systems.

ISO 23247-2 provides a manufacturing digital-twin reference architecture, while ISO 23247-4 addresses information exchange across user, service, access and proximity networks. These are useful architectural anchors for keeping agent services and industrial entities/interfaces separated. citeturn0search11turn0search15

AgentState├── identity├── intent├── spec_ref├── execution_uid├── site_scope├── asset_scope├── current_observation├── evidence_pack├── plan├── pending_approval├── tool_history├── outcomes├── escalations├── budgets└── audit_ref

Persistent state must be durable and versioned so a long-running monitoring agent can recover after service restart without accidentally repeating side effects.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 23. Output to the Next Stage
sections.content:
After the Main Agent and Toolkit complete a cycle, the next stage is generally the operational/consumer layer: Visualizer, notification/workflow systems, CMMS/MES/ERP integrations, audit/governance, or a new Runtime monitoring cycle. It should not automatically feed arbitrary outputs back into the model as truth.

Exact patch releases should be locked in the repository's dependency files and validated in CI; the versions above are a reference baseline, not a certification of compatibility.

Kubernetes-capable production environment or equivalent isolated services.

PostgreSQL for durable metadata/state.

Redis for ephemeral coordination/cache where required.

Message bus for telemetry/events.

Graph + vector + object storage services.

Model inference endpoint.

Policy engine and identity provider.

Tool Gateway with network segmentation.

Central observability and audit storage.

Site connectivity appropriate to IT/OT architecture.

Backup, disaster recovery and key management.

sections.content: CHATBOT  -> Intent Contract       |       vAGENT BUILDER  -> Agent SPEC       |       vKNOWLEDGE FOUNDATION + RUNTIME  -> Evidence / Model / Capability context       |       vMAIN AGENT  -> Toolkit calls / decisions       |       vTOOLKIT + GATEWAY  -> operational results       |       +--> VISUALIZER       +--> NOTIFICATION       +--> CMMS / MES / ERP       +--> AUDIT       +--> next monitoring cycle

Every Main Agent execution should have a correlation/execution UID. Traces should cover intent ingestion, SPEC resolution, retrieval, graph queries, telemetry reads, model calls, policy decisions, toolkit calls and final outcome. OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral framework for generating, collecting and exporting traces, metrics and logs, making it suitable for this distributed architecture. citeturn0search5turn0search7

Tenant/site/asset authorization.

Separate credentials from model context.

Input/output schema validation.

Prompt-injection-resistant authority separation.

Network segmentation for industrial integrations.

sections.heading_text: 34. Key Failure: Main Agent Becomes a Super-Agent
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 34. Key Failure: Main Agent Becomes a Super-Agent
sections.content:
Risk: a general-purpose agent accumulates dozens of connectors and begins making decisions outside its intended industrial purpose.

Mitigation: each Main Agent is purpose-bound to a signed SPEC; capabilities are allow-listed; scope is explicit; toolkit capabilities are versioned; autonomy is configurable; and the gateway rejects capabilities outside the contract.

sections.heading_text: 35. Key Failure: Toolkit Becomes a Hidden Backdoor
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 35. Key Failure: Toolkit Becomes a Hidden Backdoor
sections.content:
Risk: a toolkit capability internally invokes another powerful capability or bypasses policy.

Mitigation: every capability is registered, versioned and observable; nested calls inherit the original execution identity and scope; policy is enforced at the gateway boundary; unregistered side effects are denied.

sections.heading_text: 36. Key Failure: Automation Without Ground Truth
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 36. Key Failure: Automation Without Ground Truth
sections.content:
Risk: the Main Agent produces an impressive explanation but the underlying telemetry is stale or the procedure is obsolete.

Mitigation: Evidence Pack requires source/version/freshness metadata; configured actions require evidence thresholds; stale telemetry can force abstention; retired KB documents are excluded; model scope is validated.

sections.heading_text: 37. Key Failure: Industrialist Cannot Understand Why
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 37. Key Failure: Industrialist Cannot Understand Why
sections.content:
Risk: operators reject the system because it cannot explain the basis for an alert.

Mitigation: every important output exposes a compact reason chain: observed state → evidence → model estimate → rule/policy → capability executed → result. Visualizer markers link directly to the evidence.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 38. Key Failure: Infinite Agent Loop
sections.content:
Risk: agent repeatedly retrieves, reasons and calls tools.

Mitigation: maximum steps, wall-clock budget, tool-call budget, token budget, repeated-plan detection, circuit breakers and escalation.

sections.heading_text: 39. Proof of Concept — Compressor Health Main Agent
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 39. Proof of Concept — Compressor Health Main Agent
sections.content:
POC objective: demonstrate that an industrialist can configure a compressor-monitoring objective through Jane and receive a governed Main Agent that continuously observes, analyzes and alerts without requiring a data scientist to manually orchestrate each step.

Jane captures the intent and requested autonomy.

Agent Builder generates and signs a SPEC.

Runtime loads the SPEC and initializes Main Agent state.

Telemetry supplies vibration/temperature.

Knowledge Graph resolves COMP-02 topology and relevant components.

RAG retrieves the approved bearing procedure.

ML Studio model v2.1.0 estimates health/degradation.

Main Agent builds an evidence-backed plan.

Policy permits the configured alert capability.

Toolkit creates a maintenance alert with an idempotency key.

Visualizer displays the trend/FFT/model score and marks the triggering interval.

Audit stores the complete execution lineage.

Replay verifies deterministic safeguards and no duplicate alert.

Stale telemetry test forces abstention.

Prompt-injection test confirms retrieved text cannot expand permissions.

Unregistered work-order capability is denied.

This is an engineering readiness mapping, not a legal certification.

NIST's AI RMF and its Generative AI Profile are useful governance anchors because they organize trustworthy-AI risk management across the lifecycle. NIST also released a 2026 concept note for a Critical Infrastructure Profile, directly relevant to industrial deployments. citeturn0search0turn0search6

NIST AI RMF / Generative AI Profile: cross-sector guidance for managing trustworthy AI risks across the lifecycle. citeturn0search0

OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency: directly relevant to the Main Agent/toolkit separation because it identifies excessive functionality, permissions and autonomy as root causes of damaging agent actions. citeturn0search2

OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10: useful for treating reusable agent skills/capabilities as a distinct execution-security layer. citeturn0search9

ISO 23247-1:2021: manufacturing digital-twin framework principles. citeturn0search1

ISO 23247-2:2021: manufacturing digital-twin reference architecture. citeturn0search11

ISO 23247-4:2021: technical requirements for information exchange between entities. citeturn0search15

ISO 23247-5:2026: digital thread across the manufacturing digital-twin lifecycle, highly relevant to AI-ConneX execution/data lineage. citeturn0search3

ISO 23247-6:2026: digital twin composition and interoperability, relevant to federating multiple industrial/site capabilities. citeturn0search8

OpenTelemetry: vendor-neutral traces, metrics, logs and related observability signals for the distributed agent/toolkit architecture. citeturn0search5turn0search7

The goal is not to remove engineers. It is to remove repetitive orchestration and reduce the amount of specialist effort required for routine monitoring, evidence collection, reporting and controlled workflow management.

CHATBOT  -> user intent  -> AGENT SPEC  -> MAIN AGENT INSTANCE  -> evidence + reasoning  -> TOOLKIT CAPABILITY  -> POLICY / APPROVAL  -> TOOL GATEWAY  -> INDUSTRIAL RESULT  -> VISUALIZER / WORKFLOW / AUDIT  -> MONITORING LOOPCore rule:MAIN AGENT COORDINATES.TOOLKIT CAPABILITIES.RUNTIME ENFORCES.SPEC CONSTRAINS.POLICY AUTHORIZES.KNOWLEDGE GROUNDS.VISUALIZER EXPLAINS.AUDIT PROVES.

Every production Main Agent has a signed, versioned SPEC.

Every toolkit capability has an owner, schema, risk class and test suite.

Default-deny policy is enabled.

OT/control integrations have independent safety/authorization boundaries.

Evidence provenance is complete for consequential decisions.

Telemetry freshness requirements are tested.

Model version and scope are pinned.

Idempotency and reconciliation are tested for writes.

Prompt injection and tool-result injection tests pass.

Cross-tenant/site/asset isolation tests pass.

Agent loop budgets and kill/pause controls are operational.

Audit and OpenTelemetry coverage are production-ready.

Disaster recovery and durable-state replay have been tested.

The Main Agent is the operational brain presented to the industrialist, but it is deliberately not the security or capability boundary. The Agentic Toolkit is the industrial capability layer that turns the brain's intent into reusable, typed operations. Together they convert AI-ConneX from a collection of AI services into an operational system that can monitor, investigate, explain, alert and coordinate industrial work under explicit governance.

The strongest architectural property is separation of concerns: Jane understands intent; the Agent SPEC defines the contract; the Knowledge Foundation provides evidence; the Main Agent coordinates; the Toolkit provides capabilities; Policy authorizes; the Gateway executes; the Visualizer explains; and Audit preserves accountability.

sections.heading_text: Chapter 16: Agentic Studio Visualizer Detailed Documentation
sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 16: Agentic Studio Visualizer Detailed Documentation
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

AGENTIC STUDIO — INDUSTRIAL GROUND-STATE VISUALIZER

Detailed R&D, Architecture, Implementation, Compliance & Proof-of-Concept DocumentationReport #5 • Version 1.0 • August 2026

The Agentic Studio Visualizer is the human-facing and machine-grounded representation of an industrial environment inside AI-ConneX. It should not be treated as a conventional dashboard. Its architectural role is to establish and render an Industrial Ground-State: a current, contextual representation of assets, machines, processes, telemetry, relationships, alerts, models, agents, knowledge and permitted tools.

The Visualizer receives the user's operational intent from Jane/Chatbot and consumes lineage and intelligence produced by Data Studio and ML Studio. It transforms these inputs into a live operational view that an industrialist can understand without interpreting datasets, ML metrics, database schemas or raw telemetry.

The Visualizer is not the agent's decision engine. The Agent Runtime can consume the same Ground-State through APIs. This separation prevents the UI from becoming the system of record.

Important pipeline clarification: the Visualizer is downstream of ML Studio, while Data Profiler is upstream in Data Studio. Therefore the Visualizer's normal output is NOT an input to Data Profiler. Its primary outputs go to Agent Builder, Agent Spec, Agent Runtime, monitoring and governance. A separate, versioned operational-feedback path can later create a NEW Data Studio profiling run.

USER  |JANE / CHATBOT  |  +-------------------+  |                   |DATA STUDIO         ML STUDIO  |                   |  +---------+---------+            |      AGENTIC STUDIO            |  INDUSTRIAL GROUND-STATE            |     +------+------+     |             | VISUALIZER   GROUND-STATE API     |             | INDUSTRIALIST  AGENT BUILDER                   |             AGENT SPEC                   |             AGENT RUNTIME                   |       +-----------+-----------+       |           |           |      RAG      TELEMETRY     MODELS       |           |           |       +-----------+-----------+                   |                 TOOLS                   |             ALERT / ACT

Figure 16.1: Pipeline Connection — Visualizer Ground-Site to Agent Builder

Translate technical state into industrial context.

Give the industrialist a common view of what AI-ConneX knows.

Show where an alert originates and what it affects.

Expose live telemetry and model predictions without requiring a data scientist.

Provide an explainability surface for agent decisions.

Give Agent Builder a grounded representation of assets and capabilities.

Expose agent activity, health, permissions and pending actions.

Support human approval for actions that should not be autonomous.

Provide a visual audit trail of events and interventions.

Reduce the chance that Jane or an agent invents assets or relationships that do not exist.

The Ground-State is the canonical, versioned representation of the industrial environment as known by AI-ConneX at a point in time. The Visualizer is a projection of this state, not its source of truth.

Discover and render the Ground-State.

Provide plant → line → machine → component drill-down.

Overlay telemetry, alerts and model predictions.

Show data freshness and connection health.

Show model/version identity where predictions are displayed.

Show agent activity and pending actions.

Expose evidence behind important alerts.

Respect role, tenant, site and asset permissions.

Preserve auditability of displayed state.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 8. What It Must NOT Do
sections.content:
Train ML models.

Silently clean production data.

Invent missing assets or relationships.

Execute unrestricted industrial commands.

Treat visualization color as the actual risk calculation.

Replace the Ground-State store with browser state.

Allow an LLM to directly modify safety-critical configuration.

Hide uncertainty or stale telemetry.

Become a second Data Profiler.

PLANT | +-- LINE A       STATUS: WARNING |    +-- M01     NORMAL |    +-- M02     NORMAL |    +-- M03     HIGH RISK |         +-- Temperature: 92.4 C |         +-- Vibration: 8.71 RMS |         +-- Failure probability: 87% | +-- LINE B       STATUS: NORMAL

AI-ConneX can expose domain-specific mathematical views when they help explain operational state. The calculation engine should remain separate from the renderer.

FFT/frequency spectrum for vibration or acoustic signals.

Time-domain trends and rolling statistics.

Spectrograms where appropriate.

Control-chart style monitoring.

Correlation/relationship views.

Energy/load curves.

Threshold bands and confidence intervals.

Residual/error plots.

A mathematical visualization must carry units, sampling assumptions, method and timestamp.

FFT_RESULT+-- result_uid+-- source_stream_uid+-- sampling_rate_hz+-- window_function+-- window_size+-- overlap+-- transform_version+-- generated_at+-- source_hash

The Ground-State gives Agent Builder actual industrial context. If the user asks to monitor compressors, the builder can discover actual compressors, telemetry, models, knowledge and permitted actions rather than inventing them.

Jane | vVisualization Intent | vGround-State Query |-- Assets |-- Telemetry |-- Models |-- Knowledge |-- Tools | vAgent Builder | vAgent Spec / Blueprint

{  "agent_id": "AGT-COMP-001",  "purpose": "compressor_health_monitoring",  "assets": ["COMP-01","COMP-02","COMP-03"],  "inputs": ["temperature","pressure","vibration"],  "models": ["compressor_failure_v2"],  "knowledge": ["compressor_sop_v4"],  "triggers": ["telemetry_update","risk_score_change"],  "actions": ["create_alert","notify_maintenance"],  "approval_policy": "human_approval_for_control_actions"}

Industrial environments are fragmented across ERP, MES, SCADA, PLC/IoT systems, databases, files and human procedures. A visual layer that merely charts streams does not solve the semantic problem. AI-ConneX therefore treats visualization as a projection of a structured Ground-State that unifies operational entities, relationships, live state, models and knowledge.

Research on manufacturing digital twins and knowledge graphs supports this direction. An IFAC case study at Atlas Copco Airpower describes a cognitive digital twin using an ontology-based knowledge graph to improve manufacturing-system analysis. More recent work also explores multi-layer knowledge graphs, digital twins and explainable/agentic maintenance systems.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > Chapter 17: Agentic Studio Agent Builder Detailed Documentation
sections.content:
AI-ConneX

AGENTIC STUDIO — AGENT BUILDER

Industrial Agent Blueprint, Specification & Governance EngineR&D • Architecture • Failure Analysis • Implementation • POC • ComplianceReport #5 | Version 1.0 | 14 August 2026

Agent Builder is the design-and-compilation layer of AI-ConneX Agentic Studio. It converts a structured industrial requirement into a precise, testable, versioned and permission-aware Agent Blueprint. It does not itself perform industrial actions.

The Builder receives Jane's structured intent, the Industrial Ground-State produced around the Visualizer, Data Studio lineage and metadata, ML Studio model references, approved knowledge sources, the Tool Registry and applicable policies. It resolves the requested scope, selects or composes a template, generates a candidate plan, binds capabilities, validates constraints, runs scenario tests, and compiles an immutable Agent Specification.

The core safety boundary is deliberate: an LLM can help propose an agent plan, but it cannot grant itself industrial permissions. The compiled specification, policy engine, tool gateway, identity system and human-approval rules determine what the Agent Runtime may actually do.

DATA STUDIO --------                       ML STUDIO -------------> INDUSTRIAL GROUND-STATE                         /          |JANE / CHATBOT --------/           v                               AGENT BUILDER                                     |                         +-----------+-----------+                         |                       |                    VALIDATOR                SIMULATOR                         |                       |                         +-----------+-----------+                                     |                           AGENT SPEC / BLUEPRINT                                     |                                POLICY GATE                                     |                                AGENT RUNTIME                                     |                         OBSERVE -> REASON -> ACT                                     |                               TOOL GATEWAY                                     |                             INDUSTRIAL SYSTEMS

Figure 17.1: Pipeline Connection — Agent Builder to Agent SPEC [Blueprint]

The Visualizer establishes the operational Ground-State. Agent Builder consumes that state to construct an agent contract. Runtime consumes the contract to operate under policy.

sections.section_path: DOC-SPEC-022 > 3. Why Agent Builder Is Necessary
sections.content:
Industrialists state outcomes, not agent architectures: for example, 'watch my compressors and alert maintenance when health deteriorates'.

A conversational LLM answer is not an executable industrial contract.

Agents need explicit observation, knowledge, model, tool, action, approval, escalation and failure boundaries.

Industrial assets and capabilities must be grounded in actual site identifiers rather than inferred by a model.

Reusable agent templates reduce repeated engineering work.

Every deployed agent must be versioned and auditable.

Consequential actions need controls independent of model output.

Industrial organizations should be able to create routine monitoring and assistance agents without manually implementing every orchestration flow.

NIST AI RMF provides a voluntary framework for managing AI risks and promoting trustworthy and responsible AI across design, development, deployment and use. Its lifecycle orientation supports the Builder's explicit intended-use, risk, evaluation, governance and documentation controls. citeturn0search14

ISO 23247-2 defines a manufacturing digital-twin reference architecture with domain/entity and functional views, while ISO 23247-4 defines information-exchange requirements. These provide useful architectural precedent for structured industrial context and controlled information exchange. citeturn0search0turn0search3

The research problem is: how can natural-language industrial intent be converted into a reusable autonomous-agent specification while preserving grounding, reproducibility, security, human accountability, testability and operational safety?
